items.content: Google’s AI note-taking app, Gemini Notebook, can now pull information from the books you’ve purchased. The new “Expert Intelligence” feature allows you to bring titles from Google Play Books directly into Gemini Notebook, which means you can ask questions about the material, as well as generate plans, infographics, AI podcasts, and more based on their contents.During a briefing with The Verge, Google Labs editorial director Steven Johnson showed how you can use the tool to generate a recipe book using the information in Michael Pollan’s Food Rules. In another example, Gemini Notebook applied the knowledge from Kim Scott’s management-focused Radical Candor to answer a question about handling a difficult conversation with an employee. You’ll also be able to view the full text of the book directly in Notebook.To start, more than 100,000 books from publishers like Penguin Random House, Johns Hopkins University Press, Macmillan Publishers, O’Reilly Media, and others will support Expert Intelligence. Google also worked with 15 authors, including Pollan, Scott, Steven Pinker, and Jennifer Wallace, to create “Featured Notebooks” that each author customizes with additional source material, intro letters, and more. Titles that support the feature will have “Gemini Notebook” listed under the “Tools” badge in Google Play Books.“I’m really interested in the idea of building a collection of people whose work you really value, and kind of creating your own dream team of advisors that are just available to you wherever you go,” Johnson says.Additionally, Google built protections into Gemini Notebook to prevent other users from accessing material from books they haven’t purchased. If you share a Notebook that includes a purchased book, a user who doesn’t own the title will see it listed as a source, but they won’t be able to view the full text or information related to it. Clicking the source will direct users to Google Play Books, where they can purchase it.RelatedGemini gets notebooks to help you organize projectsGoogle is renaming NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook“We want to be able to create a space where users can bring whatever knowledge, whatever expertise they think is going to be most relevant and do it in a way that creates new revenue possibilities for authors and publishers as well,” Johnson says.Google will eventually bring this feature to AI Mode in Search and the Gemini app, both of which can already pull information from Gemini Notebook. The company also has plans to expand Expert Intelligence to support scholarly articles, magazine articles, and newspapers, according to Johnson.
items.author: Emma Roth
items.titleZh: 谷歌的人工智能笔记应用现在允许你与书籍互动
items.descriptionZh:
谷歌旗下AI笔记应用Gemini Notebook推出了一项名为“专家智能”（Expert Intelligence）的新功能，允许用户将已购买的Google Play Books电子书直接导入Notebook，从而基于书籍内容提问、生成计划、信息图、AI播客等。在《The Verge》的演示中，Google Labs编辑总监Steven Johnson展示了如何利用Michael Pollan《食物规则》中的信息生成食谱书，以及如何运用Kim Scott的管理学著作《极度坦诚》回答关于与员工进行艰难对话的问题。用户还能在Notebook中直接查看书籍全文。

初期将有超过10万本图书支持该功能，合作出版商包括Penguin Random House、Johns Hopkins University Press、Macmillan Publishers、O'Reilly Media等。Google还携手Pollan、Scott、Steven Pinker、Jennifer Wallace等15位作者打造了“精选笔记本”（Featured Notebooks），每位作者会补充额外资料、介绍信等内容。支持该功能的书籍会在Google Play Books的“工具”徽章下标注“Gemini Notebook”标识。

Johnson表示，他对构建一个由自己珍视的著作作者组成的“智囊团”概念很感兴趣，这相当于随时随地拥有理想的顾问团队。为保护版权，Google在Gemini Notebook中设置了防护机制：若用户分享包含已购书籍的笔记本，未购买该书的用户只能看到来源列表，无法查看全文或相关信息，点击来源会被引导至Google Play Books购买。

Johnson强调，该功能旨在让用户汇聚所需知识，同时为作者和出版商创造新的收入可能。未来，Google计划将该功能扩展至搜索中的AI模式及Gemini应用（两者已能从Gemini Notebook读取信息），并支持学术文章、杂志文章和报纸内容。

items.title: Jensen Huang says Nvidia achieved AGI, again — not that it matters
items.description:
On Nvidia's earnings call Wednesday, CEO Jensen Huang casually announced the company had "achieved AGI," one of the tech industry's ultimate goals some of its biggest players have spent years chasing. Almost immediately, Huang dismissed the coveted milestone as "senseless."   
He's right. For the supposed finish line of the AI race, there is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we'll know when we've actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary. 
Asked about OpenAI's pursuit of AGI, Huang said that when it comes to Nvidia, "for many tasks, we could say that we've already achieved AGI."  …
Read the full story at The Verge.
items.content: On Nvidia’s earnings call Wednesday, CEO Jensen Huang casually announced the company had “achieved AGI,” one of the tech industry’s ultimate goals some of its biggest players have spent years chasing. Almost immediately, Huang dismissed the coveted milestone as “senseless.”He’s right. For the supposed finish line of the AI race, there is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we’ll know when we’ve actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary.Asked about OpenAI’s pursuit of AGI, Huang said that when it comes to Nvidia, “for many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.” He did not provide a precise definition or benchmark, but added, “I think of all of those milestones and all those, you know, they’re kind of senseless at this point.” He also pointed to AI moving beyond responding to simple prompts to autonomous agents capable of learning new skills and improving themselves “recursively.” What really matters, Huang said, is that AI is “doing productive and useful work” and “generating profitable tokens,” with more compute producing more tokens — and, inevitably, more profit. “This is the exact phase where we’re at. Which is the reason why everybody’s leaning in.”“… for many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.”This isn’t the first time Huang has said we’ve reached AGI. In March, during an appearance on the Lex Fridman podcast, he plainly stated, “I think we’ve achieved AGI.” Huang didn’t say exactly what he meant by AGI. Fridman proposed his own oddly specific definition: an AI system that’s able to “essentially do your job,” as in start, grow, and run a successful tech company worth more than $1 billion. Walking back his earlier claims, Huang said that “the odds of 100,000 of those agents building Nvidia is zero percent.”RelatedNvidia is about to be a hundred-billion-dollar-a-quarter companyNvidia CEO Jensen Huang says ‘I think we’ve achieved AGI’AI companies are sick of their favorite buzzword — so they’re inventing new onesOver the years, other tech leaders have capitalized on the term’s fuzziness and produced a veritable grab bag of definitions and benchmarks, all orbiting the same nebulous concept: AI capable of matching or surpassing human intelligence across a broad range of domains, despite the fact that “intelligence” also doesn’t have a universally agreed-upon definition.There is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we’ll know when we’ve actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary. The definition of AGI according to OpenAI – a company founded with the explicit goal of building it – leaves a lot of room for interpretation. In its charter, OpenAI defines AGI as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” Altman himself has acknowledged that this is hardly a measurable standard, admitting last year that AGI is “not a super useful term.” Complicating matters is OpenAI’s different, financially-driven definition of AGI it worked out with Microsoft — reportedly systems that can generate at least $100 billion in profits. In a recent Time story, chief research officer Mark Chen estimated OpenAI is “80% of the way” to AGI, while Altman said that by the end of the year the company would have something he would call AGI.The fact that both AGI and its threshold remain undefined is no secret: tech leaders say so themselves, even as they make predictions predicated on it. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called AGI “imprecise,” even a “marketing term,” preferring instead to talk about “powerful AI.” Others have similarly reached for their own terms to describe broadly similar ideas. In theory, there are supposed to be distinctions between them, but in practice they all bleed together. Meta talks about “personal superintelligence,” Microsoft “humanist superintelligence,” and Amazon “useful general intelligence.” Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis has taken to talking about how we’ve arrived at the “foothills of the singularity.” And OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, who reportedly led employees in chants of “feel the AGI,” now runs a company called Safe Superintelligence.New terminology hasn’t made the meaning more tangible.New terminology hasn’t made the meaning more tangible. So long as AGI remains poorly defined and carelessly used, the whole thing is senseless. Well, unless you want a handy tool for hyping up progress. So expect the industry — Huang included — to keep the AGI talk coming. Maybe an AGI will eventually show up and tell us what AGI actually means.
items.author: Robert Hart
items.titleZh: Jensen Huang says Nvidia achieved AGI, again — not that it matters
items.descriptionZh:
英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋在周三的财报电话会议上语出惊人，宣布公司“已经实现了AGI（通用人工智能）”——这一科技行业顶级玩家们追逐多年的终极目标。然而话音刚落，他又随即否定了这一里程碑的意义，称其“毫无意义”。他的判断是对的：对于这场AI竞赛的所谓终点线，业界从未就通用人工智能的含义达成共识，更不用说如何判断我们是否真正抵达了终点，这使得“实现AGI”本身就变得同样武断。

当被问及OpenAI对AGI的追求时，黄仁勋表示，就英伟达而言，“对于许多任务，我们可以说已经实现了AGI。”他没有给出精确的定义或基准，但补充道：“我认为所有这些里程碑，你知道，在这一点上都有点毫无意义。”他还指出，AI正从响应简单提示词，演进到能够自主学习新技能并“递归式”自我改进的自主智能体。黄仁勋强调，真正重要的是AI正在“做有生产力和有用的工作”并“生成能盈利的token”，更多的算力产生更多的token——不可避免地带来更多利润。“这正是我们目前所处的阶段，也是所有人都在全力投入的原因。”

这并非黄仁勋首次宣称我们已达到AGI。今年3月，他在Lex Fridman播客节目中曾直言“我认为我们已实现了AGI”，但并未明确其含义。当时Fridman提出了一个异常具体的定义：一个能够“完成你的工作”的AI系统，即创办、发展并运营一家市值超过10亿美元的成功科技公司。黄仁勋随后收回了此前的说法，表示“10万个这样的智能体打造出英伟达的概率是零”。

多年来，其他科技领袖也充分利用了AGI这一术语的模糊性，产出了五花八门的定义和基准，但都围绕着同一个模糊概念：在广泛领域中能够匹配或超越人类智能的AI——尽管“智能”本身也没有一个被普遍接受的定义。OpenAI创立时的明确目标是构建AGI，其章程将AGI定义为“在大多数具有经济价值的工作中表现优于人类的高度自主系统”。但联合创始人兼CEO奥特曼自己也承认，这很难算是一个可衡量的标准，去年他甚至表示AGI“不是一个非常有用的术语”。更复杂的是，OpenAI与微软之间达成了一套以财务为导向的AGI定义——据报道是指能够创造至少1000亿美元利润的系统。在最近《时代》杂志的报道中，OpenAI首席研究官马克·陈估计公司已“完成了通向AGI的80%”，而奥特曼则表示到年底公司会拥有他称之为AGI的东西。

AGI及其门槛都未被定义这一事实并非秘密：科技领袖们自己就承认了这一点，即便他们仍基于此做出预测。Anthropic CEO达里奥·阿莫德伊称AGI“不精确”，甚至是“营销术语”，他更倾向于谈论“强大AI”。其他公司也各自创造了术语来描述大致相似的概念——理论上它们应有区别，但实际上已混为一谈：Meta谈论“个人超级智能”，微软谈“人本超级智能”，亚马逊谈“实用通用智能”。谷歌DeepMind的戴密斯·哈萨比斯则常谈论我们已抵达“奇点的山麓”。OpenAI联合创始人伊利亚·苏茨克维——据报道曾带领员工高呼“感受AGI”——如今经营着一家名为“安全超级智能”的公司。

但新的术语并未让含义变得更加具体。只要AGI仍然定义不清、使用随意，整件事就毫无意义——除非你想要一个方便的工具来炒作进展。因此可以预见，包括黄仁勋在内的整个行业会继续大谈AGI。也许有一天，一个真正的AGI会出现，并告诉我们AGI到底意味着什么。

items.title: Trump administration weighs expanding chip tariffs to laptops, consoles, and servers, report claims — January's data center exemptions may be scrapped
items.description: The Trump administration is weighing a second round of semiconductor tariffs that would extend duties beyond chips to products built with them.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 14 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Trump administration is weighing a second round of semiconductor tariffs that would extend duties beyond chips to products built with them, including laptops, gaming consoles, and data center servers, eight unnamed sources familiar with the talks told POLITICO in a report published today. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick favors a structure that would cap duty-free chip imports at a volume pegged to each company's committed U.S. production, four of the sources said, and Commerce officials have indicated in private talks that the exemptions attached to January's 25% tariff, which cover data centers, R&D, startups, and consumer devices, may not carry over. A phase-in period is under discussion, and the framework could still change substantially in the coming weeks.Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc)While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply marketThe state of China's decade-long semiconductor pushHuawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fabChina's latest round of rare-earth export controls explainedProclamation 11002, signed on January 14, imposed a 25% duty on a narrow set of advanced accelerators, with Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X named in the accompanying White House fact sheet, and explicitly labeled the action Phase 1.The same document directed Commerce to report to the president by July 1 on the market for semiconductors used in U.S. data centers, and a separate April 14 report from the USTR and Commerce covered tariff negotiations with Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan. The exemption categories now in question match those written into the January action and include U.S. data centers, research and development, startups, repairs, non-data-center consumer and industrial applications, and public sector uses.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Taiwan's January trade agreement applies zero tariffs on Taiwanese chips within 2.5 times a company's current U.S. manufacturing capacity while new plants are under construction, tightening to 1.5 times once they're built. TSMC has committed $265 billion to its Arizona site, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history, yet projects only around 30% of its most advanced capacity there at full build-out, according to POLITICO. Taiwan produces more than 90% of the world's leading-edge chips, and industry representatives argued in the talks that a quota keyed to current domestic capacity can't cover the volumes hyperscalers are buying during a record AI spending run.Jonathan McHale, digital policy chief at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, whose members include Amazon, Google, and Meta, compared the data center buildout to "building the transcontinental railroad" and said added cost and unpredictability put that investment at risk. You may like Taiwan weighs criminal ban on AI chip exports to all of China While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market Industry coalition urges Trump administration to take urgent action as AI data centers' extreme memory consumption threatens other industries Tech lobbyists have met with Lutnick and Bureau of Industry and Security undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler with growing frequency since the start of summer, per the report, but three of the sources said recent talks moved against the industry. One person involved put the domestic manufacturing build-out at more than five years, longer than any phase-in the administration has allowed on previous tariff rounds.White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the approach, saying reshoring chip manufacturing is a top priority for the president; the Commerce Department didn't respond to POLITICO's requests for comment.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
items.author: Luke James
items.titleZh: 报道称特朗普政府考虑将芯片关税扩大至笔记本电脑、游戏机和服务器——1月的数据中心豁免或被取消
items.descriptionZh:
特朗普政府正酝酿第二轮半导体关税，其范围将从芯片本身扩展至使用芯片的终端产品，包括笔记本电脑、游戏主机和数据中心服务器。据POLITICO今日报道，八位匿名知情人士透露了相关讨论细节。商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克倾向于一种配额机制：以各企业承诺的美国本土产量为基准，设定一个免税芯片进口上限，超过部分需缴纳关税。商务部官员在私下会谈中还暗示，今年1月25%关税中附带的多项豁免——涵盖数据中心、研发、初创企业及消费设备——可能不会延续。目前正在讨论分阶段实施的时间表，但整个框架在未来数周内仍可能发生重大变化。

这场关税风波源于1月14日签署的第11002号公告，该公告对一小部分先进加速器征收25%关税，英伟达H200和AMD MI325X被明确点名，白宫称其为“第一阶段”行动。该公告同时要求商务部在7月1日前向总统提交关于美国数据中心所用半导体市场的报告，而4月14日美国贸易代表办公室和商务部联合发布的报告则涉及与台湾、韩国和日本的关税谈判。如今受到质疑的豁免类别，正是1月行动中写入的那些，包括美国数据中心、研发、初创企业、维修、非数据中心消费与工业应用以及公共部门用途。

台湾方面，1月签署的贸易协议规定，在新建工厂建设期间，台湾芯片可享受相当于企业当前美国产能2.5倍进口量的零关税待遇，工厂建成后这一倍数将收紧至1.5倍。台积电已承诺向亚利桑那州投资2650亿美元，这是美国历史上最大规模的外国直接投资，但据POLITICO报道，其最先进产能全面投产后，在美占比也仅约30%。台湾生产了全球超过90%的先进制程芯片。行业代表在谈判中指出，在AI支出创纪录的当下，以现有国内产能为基准的配额，根本无法覆盖超大规模云服务商的采购量。

计算机与通信行业协会（CCIA）数字政策主管乔纳森·麦克海尔将数据中心建设比作“建造横贯大陆的铁路”，并表示额外成本和不可预测性正使这项投资面临风险。该协会成员包括亚马逊、谷歌和Meta。自入夏以来，科技游说团体与卢特尼克及工业与安全局副局长杰弗里·凯斯勒的会面频率不断上升，但三位知情人士称，最近的会谈风向对行业不利。一位参与者指出，美国本土制造能力的全面构建需要五年以上，这远超此前各轮关税中政府允许的任何分阶段过渡期。

白宫发言人库什·德赛为这一做法辩护，称将芯片制造回流是美国总统的首要任务；商务部则未回应POLITICO的置评请求。这场围绕关税结构、豁免范围和实施节奏的博弈，不仅将决定芯片进口成本，更可能重塑全球半导体供应链格局——尤其是对高度依赖台湾先进制程的英伟达、AMD等美国芯片巨头，以及大规模采购AI加速器的云计算产业。特朗普政府此番“芯片+终端”双重关税的设计，名义上旨在强制推动制造业回流，但其对AI基础设施投资、消费电子价格乃至全球科技产业链的连锁影响，仍有待观察。

items.title: Hot Chips 2026: Cerebras lays out the future of wafer-scale AI — Nexus system architecture triples rack-scale performance, CS-6 wafer to incorporate stacked DRAM
items.description: At Hot Chips 2026, Cerebras revealed the next two generations of its wafer-scale accelerator roadmap. It also discussed the benefits of its new Nexus rack design for the CS-4 rack-scale accelerator and the performance of the three WS-3T wafer-scale engines contained within.
items.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Cerebras' SRAM-packed wafer-scale engines (WSEs) have carved out a niche in the AI model serving space for extremely low-latency, high-throughput inference, enabling services like OpenAI's ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast tier. At Hot Chips 2026, the company revealed the next two generations of its wafer-scale accelerator roadmap. It also discussed the benefits of its new Nexus rack design for the CS-4 rack-scale accelerator and the performance of the three WS-3T wafer-scale engines contained within.The integration of a huge coherent processor on a single massive slice of silicon is a unique feat in the industry. But that approach also comes with limitations. AI demands for memory are only increasing due to growing model sizes (the memory occupancy of which can be amortized across multiple inference sessions) and ever-lengthening contexts stored in large KV caches (which are also unique to each inference session).Traditional GPU makers have addressed those pressures, in part by working with memory makers to stack HBM higher and by using more of it per accelerator to expand that precious resource in proximity to the processor. But on a wafer-scale design whose area is already 100% utilized by logic and memory, adding more of a particular resource requires giving up area that might have been used for some other purpose. Since silicon production will continue to take place on 300mm wafers for the foreseeable future, Cerebras must look in other directions to scale up the on-chip resources available to its processors.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: (Image credit: Cerebras)Cerebras revealed that it will start expanding its wafer-scale engines into stacked designs with its CS-6 system’s WSE, currently two generations out on its roadmap. For the first time, Cerebras will attempt 3D stacking of DRAM on top of its logic and SRAM wafer, a move it claims will maintain the company's performance lead for inference while reducing the area required for the overall chip.The goal of stacking wafer-scale logic and memory chips on top of one another is certainly ambitious, but it’s only one potentially important change in the CS-6 system. The concurrent reduction in area Cerebras foresees suggests the company might be able to increase the overall number of WSEs it produces, which could relax a crucial constraint as the company seeks to scale its business amid a world of ever-increasing wafer demand. You may like AMD and Cerebras partner on low-latency, high-throughput AI inference Hot Chips 2026: d-Matrix stacks AI accelerator directly on custom DRAM for 100 TB/s per card Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia presents Groq 3 LPX architecture and unveils its first third-party inference benchmark (Image credit: Cerebras)In the present, Cerebras is boosting the performance of its existing wafer-scale platform with its new CS-4 rack-scale system and its Nexus rack design. CS-4 incorporates three of the company's refreshed WS-3T wafers into self-contained "backpacks" that incorporate power delivery, scale-up networking, and liquid cooling infrastructure into a single pluggable module. (Image credit: Cerebras)Cerebras notes that because these modules are self-contained, future wafer-scale engines built with this architecture can be swapped in without exchanging the entire rack in the process.Cerebras chief system architect JP Fricker had choice words when describing the 5,000 cables that are used to connect the Rubin NVL72 NVLink scale-up domain within each of those racks, calling it "a mess" and contrasting it with the cleaner and less failure-prone design provided by the on-die interconnects and self-contained compute module design of the Nexus system. (Image credit: Cerebras)The Nexus backpack design also disaggregates the I/O interfaces of the WSE from the rest of the backpack's components. Two I/O modules now connect to the edges of the wafer, providing RoCE v2 RDMA connections for interoperability with other systems, alongside a direct connection to other wafers in the rack. Because these modules are also interchangeable, they provide another potential route for future upgrades, independent of the core compute wafer. (Image credit: Cerebras)The Nexus design situates up to 10 rack power delivery units for each backpack at the front side of the rack, each group of which can be configured for varying levels of redundancy in accordance with an operator’s needs. The rack also provides air cooling for the backpack components that need it. What to read next Hot Chips 2026: Intel dives deep on Crescent Island AI accelerator TSMC says panel packaging won't replace CoWoS anytime soon for the largest future AI processors Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia breaks down 88-core Vera CPU (Image credit: Cerebras)Mounting the wafer-scale engines vertically in the backpack modules lets Cerebras do away with a PCB or substrate for the wafer to handle all its supporting infrastructure. Instead, the backpack connects the large copper busbar that delivers juice to the chip directly to its back side. This close contact is important, as it minimizes power losses that occur on the way to the chip, as happens with a BGA GPU chip mounted on a PCB module with all of its power delivery circuitry located around the die.Cerebras translates the power saved this way directly into performance in the WS-3T. The company says the losses avoided by the Nexus backpack design allow it to deliver twice as much power to the wafer-scale engine as in past designs, which leads directly to increased clock speeds and up to twice the performance of the WS-3. (Image credit: Cerebras)Using the same base silicon as the WS-3, each WS-3T delivers twice as many sparse FP16 petaFLOPS and twice as much memory bandwidth from its SRAM. But the WS3-T is still limited to 44GB of memory across the entire wafer, and three such wafers in a CS-4 rack only scale up to 132 GB, far less than the 20.7 TB of HBM in the Vera Rubin NVL72 system and the 31 TB of AMD’s Helios.The company doesn’t publish dense PFLOPS figures for these engines, possibly because the dataflow architectural design of the chips is specifically built to derive advantage from sparsity in a way a traditional GPU usually isn’t. (Image credit: Cerebras)In any event, to accommodate the larger models of today and tomorrow, Cerebras will need to scale up and out. But unlike other rack-scale systems that rely on Ethernet for scale-out, Cerebras can simply connect CS-4 systems together using the same wafer-to-wafer interconnect that connects wafer-scale engines together in the Nexus rack. The company claims 2.4 Tb/s of direct scale-up bandwidth per wafer within the rack for a total of 7.2 Tb/s of inter-chip bandwidth at 2 μs latencies.Cerebras notes that with its architecture, only the model activations need to pass between wafer-scale engines, so the relatively low bandwidth of the direct wafer connection isn't the obstacle to scaling out the system that it might seem when evaluated against the hundreds of terabytes per second of scale-up bandwidth of a system like Vera Rubin NVL72 or AMD's Helios. (The on-die fabric of the WSE-3T boasts 53.4 PB/s of bandwidth, regardless.) (Image credit: Cerebras)The CS-4 system architecture lays the groundwork for the next-generation CS-5 accelerator, which will use new WSE silicon in 2027. For smaller models, the company says the next-generation WSE will deliver up to 10,000 tokens per second per user, while larger frontier models from labs like DeepSeek or OpenAI could run at 5,000 tokens per second per user.As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said, AI agents are impatient, and the ability to provide such vast numbers of tokens per second using specialized accelerators like the CS-4 will likely continue to be an important niche for Cerebras to exploit alongside its partners at OpenAI and AMD going forward. items.titleZh: Hot Chips 2026: Cerebras lays out the future of wafer-scale AI — Nexus system architecture triples rack-scale performance, CS-6 wafer to incorporate stacked DRAM
items.descriptionZh:
在Hot Chips 2026大会上，Cerebras揭开了其晶圆级加速器未来两代产品路线图的面纱，并详细展示了其新一代CS-4机架级加速系统与Nexus机架设计的底层创新。Cerebras以其独特的晶圆级引擎（WSE）在AI模型推理服务市场中占据了一席之地，凭借极低延迟和高吞吐量的特性，为OpenAI的ChatGPT-5.6 Sol超快速服务等级等尖端应用提供了算力支撑。此次发布的核心在于，面对AI模型规模和上下文长度持续攀升带来的内存压力，Cerebras正在开辟一条与传统GPU厂商截然不同的演进路径。

长期以来，Cerebras的独门绝技是将一个巨大的、拥有高度一致性互连的处理器集成在一整片硅晶圆上，这在业内独一无二。但这一方案也受制于一个根本性约束：晶圆面积是固定的，且已被逻辑和SRAM存储完全占满。随着模型尺寸增长（其内存占用可在多次推理会话间分摊）和KV缓存随上下文不断拉长（且每次会话独享），AI对内存的需求水涨船高。传统GPU厂商通过堆叠更高层的HBM或增加单卡HBM容量来扩充处理器附近的高速存储，而Cerebras不能简单地在晶圆上“挤出”更多空间——增加某类资源就意味着牺牲其他功能单元的面积。由于半导体制造在可预见的未来仍将采用300mm晶圆，Cerebras必须寻找其他途径来扩展片上资源。

为此，Cerebras宣布将在其路线图中两代之后的CS-6系统中，首次尝试将DRAM以3D堆叠方式直接集成在包含逻辑与SRAM的晶圆之上。该公司声称，这一激进举措将维持其在推理领域的性能领先地位，同时缩小整体芯片的占地面积。面积的缩减还带来一个战略性的连锁好处：有可能提高WSE的总产量，从而缓解在全球晶圆需求持续暴涨背景下制约公司规模化的关键瓶颈。

着眼当下，Cerebras正通过全新的CS-4机架级系统和Nexus机架设计，将现有晶圆级平台的性能推向更高水平。CS-4系统集成了三片经过升级的WS-3T晶圆，每片晶圆被封装进一个自成一体的“背包装甲”模块中，该模块将供电、横向扩展网络和液冷基础设施全部整合进一个可插拔的单元。这种设计使得未来新一代晶圆级引擎能够直接替换升级，而无需更换整个机架。Cerebras首席系统架构师JP Fricker在描述对比时措辞犀利，他将Nvidia Rubin NVL72机架内连接NVLink横向扩展域所需的5000根线缆称为“一团乱麻”，并强调Nexus系统通过片上互连和自包含计算模块设计实现了更整洁、更不易故障的架构。

Nexus背板设计还实现了I/O接口与模块其他组件的解耦。两个I/O模块连接至晶圆边缘，提供RoCE v2 RDMA连接以实现与其他系统的互操作，同时还能直接连接机架内的其他晶圆。这些I/O模块同样可互换，为核心计算晶圆之外的未来升级提供了另一条独立路径。供电方面，每个背板模块最多可配置10个机架电源单元，分布于机架前侧，可根据运营商需求灵活配置冗余等级；机架同时为需要空气冷却的组件提供散热支持。

其中一个细节尤为精妙：将晶圆级引擎垂直安装在背板模块中，使得Cerebras能够省去传统的PCB或基板来承载支撑基础设施。取而代之的是，背板将一根粗壮的铜母线直接连到晶圆背面，为芯片供电。这种紧密接触至关重要，因为它极大减少了电力在传输路径上的损耗——相比传统BGA封装的GPU芯片需要安装在PCB模块上、供电电路分布于芯片周围的方式，铜母线直供大大降低了压降。Cerebras将这种节省下来的电力空间直接转化为性能提升：Nexus背板设计避免了损耗，使得传给晶圆级引擎的功率达到以往设计的两倍，直接带来核心频率的提升，使WS-3T的性能达到WS-3的两倍。

在具体规格上，WS-3T与WS-3采用相同的底层硅片，但其稀疏FP16峰值性能（以petaFLOPS计）和SRAM内存带宽均翻倍。然而，WS-3T在整个晶圆上依然只有44GB的片上存储，即使CS-4机架内三片晶圆也不过132GB，与Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72的20.7TB HBM以及AMD Helios的31TB相比，简直是天壤之别。Cerebras没有公布这些引擎的密集计算性能指标，这很可能是因为其芯片的数据流架构专为利用稀疏性而设计，而传统GPU通常无法从稀疏性中获得同等收益。

面对未来更大规模的模型，Cerebras需要同时向上和向外扩展。与其他依赖以太网进行横向扩展的机架级系统不同，Cerebras可以直接使用Nexus机架内连接晶圆级引擎的晶圆间互连，将多个CS-4系统连接起来。公司声称，机架内每片晶圆可提供2.4Tb/s的直连横向扩展带宽，总片间带宽达7.2Tb/s，延迟低至2微秒。Cerebras指出，由于其架构的特殊性，晶圆级引擎之间只需传递模型激活值（activations），而非权重或完整KV缓存，因此相比Vera Rubin NVL72或AMD Helios那数百TB/s的横向扩展带宽，直连晶圆连接看似“低”的带宽并不会成为系统扩展的瓶颈。毕竟，WS-3T的片上互连本身已拥有高达53.4PB/s的带宽。

CS-4系统架构为采用全新WSE硅片的下一代CS-5加速器（预计2027年问世）奠定了坚实基础。Cerebras表示，对于较小的模型，下一代WSE可为每位用户提供高达每秒10,000个token的生成速度；而对于DeepSeek或OpenAI等实验室开发的大型前沿模型，每位用户也能达到每秒5,000个token。正如Nvidia CEO黄仁勋所言，“AI代理没有耐心”，能够借助CS-4这类专用加速器提供如此海量的token生成速率，或将继续成为Cerebras与OpenAI、AMD等伙伴合作中的关键差异化优势。Cerebras通过Nexus机架对供电和封装的革新，加上未来两代产品中3D DRAM堆叠的宏大蓝图，展现了其在AI算力竞赛中另辟蹊径、以单晶圆极限性能制胜的坚定决心。

items.title: Nvidia expects to sell $20 billion of Vera Rubin systems in Q3 as shipments begin — figure would account for 20% of its data center revenue mix, marks fastest ramp in company history
items.description: Nvidia expects Vera Rubin to become its fastest-ramping data center AI platform as it projects sales of Vera Rubin hardware to hit 20% of data center revenue in its third fiscal quarter.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Nvidia expects sales of the Vera Rubin platform to account for around 20% of its data center revenue in the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which will make it the company's fastest-ramping data center product in history. As Nvidia projects its revenue to be around $108 billion in Q3 FY2027, sales of Vera Rubin hardware alone will total around $20 billion in just one quarter.Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft)The data center cooling state of playThe custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the priceGTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this yearDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible"We see Vera Rubin accounting for about 20% of data center revenue in Q3," said Colette Kress, chief financial officer at Nvidia, during the company's earnings conference call with financial analysts and investors. "Having already received purchase orders from every major hyperscaler, AI cloud, and system OEM, we expect Vera Rubin to mark the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history."Data center revenue has accounted for around 92% of Nvidia's quarterly sales in recent quarters, so as long as Nvidia meets its $108 billion earnings projection in Q3, its data center revenue will reach around $99.36 billion, meaning that sales of its Vera Rubin platform hardware will be around $19.872 billion.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Nvidia began to ramp up production of Vera Rubin components — that include Vera CPUs, Rubin GPUs, BlueField 4 DPUs, and other units — this spring and commenced first revenue shipments of actual VR200 NVL72 racks in August, with Microsoft being the first to deploy commercial systems (at least according to Satya Nadella).Normally, companies ramp up production and sales of their data center platforms for several quarters. Ramping up a data center platform from effectively no production revenue in Q2 FY2027 to 20% of revenue ($20 billion in this case) in just one quarter is a record not only for Nvidia, but perhaps for the whole industry, given Nvidia's scale. However, there is a catch: actual unit shipments do not look truly breakthrough. You may like Nvidia revenue tops $96 billion as memory commitments soar to $160 billion Nvidia's Huang vows to deliver 'giant amounts' of Vera Rubin — company says that 'our roadmap is intact' Nvidia deep dives Vera CPU for AI data centers Exact volumes of Vera Rubin units that Nvidia plans to ship in the third quarter of its fiscal 2027 are unknown. However, if Nvidia ships only VR200 NVL72 rack-scale systems, depending on their actual price and configuration (estimated from $5 million to $7.8 million per unit), Nvidia will supply from roughly 2,550 to approximately 3,975 machines containing 91,700 – 143,100 Vera CPUs as well as 183,500 – 286,100 Rubin GPUs.These numbers are, of course, very rough since the company will sell a boatload of MGX servers and even Vera CPUs and Rubin GPUs separately, meaning that actual unit shipment volumes of these key components will be higher. Nonetheless, we are still talking about hundreds of thousands, rather than millions, of CPUs and GPUs, which is not particularly many. Still, given the stellar prices of leading-edge AI hardware, even relatively limited volumes of these components can generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.

items.titleZh: Nvidia expects to sell $20 billion of Vera Rubin systems in Q3 as shipments begin — figure would account for 20% of its data center revenue mix, marks fastest ramp in company history
items.descriptionZh:
英伟达首席财务官科莱特·克雷斯在公司财报电话会议上宣布，该公司预计Vera Rubin平台将在2027财年第三季度贡献数据中心营收的约20%。鉴于英伟达该季度营收预期高达1080亿美元，这意味着仅Vera Rubin硬件一个季度的销售额就将达到约200亿美元，这一业绩将使其成为英伟达历史上爬坡速度最快的数据中心产品。

数据中心业务在英伟达近几个季度的总营收中占比约为92%。按照1080亿美元的营收预期计算，数据中心营收将达到约993.6亿美元，其中Vera Rubin平台硬件销售额约为198.7亿美元。据克雷斯透露，英伟达已收到所有主要超大规模云服务商、AI云厂商和系统OEM厂商的采购订单。

从产品架构来看，Vera Rubin平台是英伟达下一代AI数据中心计算平台，集成了多个核心组件：Vera CPU作为中央处理器、Rubin GPU作为加速计算单元，以及BlueField 4 DPU作为数据处理单元。英伟达于今年春季开始提升这些组件的量产规模，并在8月启动了VR200 NVL72机架级系统的首批营收出货，微软成为首家部署商用系统的客户（这一信息来自微软CEO萨蒂亚·纳德拉）。

从行业视角审视，企业通常需要多个季度才能逐步提升数据中心平台的产量和销量。而从2027财年第二季度实质上为零的产量，到第三季度跃升至营收占比20%（约200亿美元），这一爬坡速度不仅创下英伟达自身纪录，考虑到其庞大的体量，在整个行业范围内也可能是前所未有的。

然而，一个值得关注的细节是：实际的单元出货量数据似乎并未展现出真正的突破性。虽然英伟达计划在2027财年第三季度出货的确切Vera Rubin单元数量尚未公开，但根据估算，若仅以VR200 NVL72机架级系统计算——每套系统价格在500万至780万美元之间——英伟达将交付约2,550至3,975台机器，对应的Vera CPU数量为91,700至143,100颗，Rubin GPU数量为183,500至286,100颗。当然，这些数字仅为粗略估算，因为英伟达还将同时销售大量MGX服务器以及独立的Vera CPU和Rubin GPU，实际关键组件的出货量会更高。但总体而言，讨论的规模是数十万颗而非数百万颗CPU和GPU，数量并不算特别巨大。

不过，正是由于尖端AI硬件的高昂定价，即便相对有限的出货量也能产生数百亿美元的收入。这一现象折射出当前AI算力市场的核心特征：在生成式AI和大模型训练需求持续爆发的背景下，高端AI加速硬件的单位价值极高，头部厂商凭借技术领先优势可以在有限出货量的情况下实现惊人的营收规模。对于整个行业而言，Vera Rubin的快速爬坡也标志着AI数据中心的算力供给正在进入一个新的代际更替周期，后续其性能表现和实际部署效果仍值得密切关注。

items.title: Many talks between data center developers and local governments are wrapped in secrecy behind non-disclosure agreements — residents question the need for NDAs, but developers argue it’s important to avoid ‘running afoul of insider trading rules’
items.description: Researchers discovered that most negotiations between data centers and local governments are protected by NDAs. These documents keep details in secret, with residents having a difficult time finding information about these projects because of the agreements.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 5 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Researchers from the University of Mary Washington in Virginia found that of the 31 localities with an existing, approved, or proposed data center, 25 of them have non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) that make it difficult, if not impossible, for their citizens to find information about these projects. According to NPR, these NDAs have left the questions of many residents unanswered, making them feel left out of the decision process and increasing their distrust of their leaders.Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft)The data center cooling state of playThe custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the priceGTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this yearDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleMany officials defended signing these secrecy agreements, saying that this is standard practice among tech companies, and that they could lose the potential business and revenue that data center projects could bring to their jurisdiction if they fail to sign the NDA. Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois even told the publications that NDAs are “fundamental for economic development” as they allow the state to compete with other states and territories for the data centers’ business. “The last thing that they want to have happened in the beginning of the discussion, or in any part of the discussion, is for their information that they’re sharing to be disclosed publicly. So, without NDAs, our work, frankly, just doesn’t happen,” the agency secretary said to NPR. She also added, “The irony is that we, we use NDAs not to be more cloaked, we use NDAs to be more forthcoming.”NDAs aren’t only limited to Louisiana, as other towns across the U.S. have signed these secrecy agreements even before they started talks with potential data center projects in their regions. Some Wisconsin citizens raised a similar issue in early 2026, when at least four municipalities reportedly signed NDAs with Microsoft and Meta as they negotiated with the two companies. These confidentiality agreements are some of the things that drive the heated debate between elected officials and ordinary citizens, with the latter often feeling betrayed and sold out by the former when they belatedly find out that a data center will be put up in their community.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: However, West Feliciana Parish proved that it could get a data center deal without keeping its details top secret. Parish President Kenny Havard said that economic development does not require NDAs. “I don’t think NDAs are necessary unless they’re going to bring you in a room and share some proprietary information. When you’re talking about land sales, tax incentives, those sorts of things that affect the citizens, it should be out in the open. It should be transparent,” Havard told the outlet. He also said, “We’re proud that we did it without having to sign NDAs. And I think it just shows that you can do these projects without keeping the people in the dark.” Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds. items.titleZh: Many talks between data center developers and local governments are wrapped in secrecy behind non-disclosure agreements — residents question the need for NDAs, but developers argue it’s important to avoid ‘running afoul of insider trading rules’
items.descriptionZh:
美国弗吉尼亚大学玛丽·华盛顿分校的研究人员发现，在全美31个已有、已批准或拟建数据中心的地方行政辖区中，有25个签署了保密协议（NDA），这使得当地居民几乎不可能了解这些项目的具体信息。据NPR报道，这些保密协议让许多居民的疑问得不到解答，使他们感到被排斥在决策过程之外，对地方领导人的不信任感也随之上升。

许多官员为签署这些保密协议辩护，称这是科技公司之间的标准做法，如果不签，他们可能会失去数据中心项目为本地区带来的潜在商业机会和税收收入。路易斯安那州经济发展部长苏珊·布尔乔亚甚至对媒体表示，NDA“对经济发展至关重要”，因为它能让该州与其他州和地区竞争数据中心的落户。“他们最不希望发生在讨论初期或任何讨论环节中的事情，就是自己分享的信息被公开披露。所以，坦率地说，没有NDA，我们的工作根本没法开展。”她还补充道：“讽刺的是，我们使用NDA不是为了更加遮遮掩掩，而是为了更加坦诚。”然而，这种说法很难让普通民众信服。

NDA并不局限于路易斯安那州，美国其他城镇甚至在开始与潜在的数据中心项目洽谈之前就签署了这类保密协议。2026年初，威斯康星州也出现了类似争议——据报道，至少有四个市镇在与微软和Meta谈判时签署了NDA。这些保密协议正是民选官员与普通公民之间激烈争论的焦点之一。居民往往在事后才得知自己社区将建设数据中心，感到被背叛和被出卖。

不过，西费利西亚纳教区证明了，不将细节保密同样能达成数据中心交易。该教区主席肯尼·哈瓦德表示，经济发展并不需要NDA。“我认为，除非对方会把你带进一个房间分享专有信息，否则NDA没有必要。当涉及土地出售、税收优惠这类影响公民切身利益的事项时，就应该公开透明。”他还说：“我们很自豪，在不签署NDA的情况下完成了这个项目。这表明，你完全可以在不让民众蒙在鼓里的前提下推进这些项目。”

items.title: Enterprise AI's real risk isn't autonomous agents. It's the complexity between them.
items.description:
Presented by Gravitee 

Agent complexity is the insidious shadow lurking inside enterprises right now that needs a light shone on it.
That’s because enterprises don't deploy a single agent and watch it run, they deploy fleets, each one calling APIs, calling other agents, reaching into applications that were never built with a machine decision-maker in mind. That's the failure mode that should keep you up at night: a windy, complicated system nobody can see clearly enough to govern. But why do things get so opaque so quickly?
Add a second agent to a system, and you've added one connection. Add a tenth, and you haven't added ten connections, you've potentially added dozens, because now any agent might call any other, and each of those calls can trigger a call somewhere else. Complexity doesn't creep up with agent headcount. It compounds with the number of paths between agents, and nobody's job is to draw that graph. A support ticket that used to touch one system might now pass through four agents before a human ever lays eyes on it, and every one of those handoffs is a decision point nobody approved.
Most enterprise AI programs stall when the humans responsible for their agents lose the thread. Ask a security team a simple question: which agents can reach which systems, and watch the silence. Ask which agent triggered which downstream action three hops ago. More silence.
The instinct is to treat this like a checklist. Approve the agent. Log the agent. Move on. I'd argue this is the wrong instinct. A checklist checks a single point in time. Complexity runs across a chain, and you can't govern a chain with a stack of one-time approvals any more than you can call a diet successful because you had a vegetable once.
So where does it actually break down?
Permissions creep first. Somebody builds an agent to summarize support tickets, grants it broad API access because scoping it properly would've taken another sprint, and forgets about it. Six months later, that same agent has a path into the payments system. Nobody remembers signing off on that. Nobody did.
And ownership thins out the further the chain runs. Five agents touch one workflow, something breaks at step four, and now you're asking who's responsible for a link nobody was ever assigned to own, because the org chart stopped at "deploy the agent" and never got to "name the human who answers for it."
This is a story about governance infrastructure that hasn't caught up with how agents actually behave: interconnected, cascading, multiplying faster than the processes built to track them.
Fixing the cluster starts with identity. Every agent needs to exist as its own entity, not a shadow permission borrowed from whoever deployed it. Its own name in the register. Its own scoped authority. A named human sponsor who answers for what it does. That part is necessary.
But it is nowhere near sufficient.
The harder piece is the oversight that holds across the entire chain, not just at each individual link in it. You need to see what an agent did, what it set off downstream, and where that trail ends in real time, not in a report someone pulls together once a quarter. Get agent-level identity right and stop there, and you end up with a filing cabinet full of perfectly documented agents operating inside a system nobody can actually explain.
And oversight by itself only tells you what already happened. Watching a chain isn't the same as controlling it. Enforcement is the piece most programs skip: the ability to stop an out-of-policy call before it executes, not just log it for someone to find in a review three weeks later. A dashboard that shows you an agent breached its scope five minutes ago is a monitoring tool. A system that stops the breach from happening in the first place is governance. Enterprises serious about agent accountability need both, and most have only built the first.
We're all running at blazing speed to ensure we're not the ones left behind in the race we've found ourselves in, and we're all too aware that there's a cost to slowing down. Every enterprise serious about agentic AI hits the complexity wall eventually. The ones that get past it are the ones who built enough visibility and accountability, so their fleet can keep growing without anyone losing the ability to answer one question: what is this system doing right now, and who's responsible for it.
But don't miss the point. Complexity isn't a reason to pump the brakes. The enterprises getting this right aren't slowing down. They're building toward Human-Agent Harmony, where scale and accountability grow together instead of trading off against each other.
The real risk was never a single agent doing exactly what it was built to do. It's a hundred of them doing exactly that, all at once, interacting in combinations nobody designed for. That kind of multiplication is what keeps enterprise AI stuck running pilots forever instead of running production.
Solve for complexity and autonomy stops being the villain. It starts being the whole point.
Rory Blundell is CEO at Gravitee.
