items.titleZh: EPA faces lawsuit over claims it fast-tracked approval of toxic 'data center chemicals' — exposure to photoacid generators used for semiconductor manufacturing could result in ‘sudden death,’ also appear to be long-lasting PFAS
items.descriptionZh:
美国环境保护署（EPA）近期批准了两种新化学品在美国境内使用，但非营利组织Earthjustice随即提起诉讼，指控EPA未能履行其法定职责。据《卫报》报道，这两种化学品是用于半导体制造的光酸产生剂（photoacid generators），但同时对人体具有相当高的毒性。接触这些物质可能导致“猝死”，并引发癌症、眼部腐蚀、神经系统损伤及生殖危害等多种健康风险。诉讼方指出，这些批准“是围绕数据中心问题的更广泛模式的一部分”。

这两种化学品在半导体光刻工艺中扮演关键角色：光酸产生剂是光刻胶的核心组分，在曝光后产生酸，从而在晶圆上形成精细的电路图案。然而，其毒性不容忽视。Earthjustice的律师Jonathan Kalmuss-Katz表示，EPA“并不清楚这些化学品达到何种浓度才会‘急性致命’或造成其他严重健康损害”，并指出“这些化学品可能对工人和公众构成‘不合理的风险’”。尽管如此，EPA仍以最低限度且无保护性的限制条件批准了其进口和使用。

Kalmuss-Katz援引《有毒物质控制法》（TSCA）强调，若一种化学品可能构成“不合理的风险”，EPA必须“禁止或限制其制造、加工、商业分销、使用或处置，或组合限制这些活动，以在必要程度上防范该风险”。他批评道：“这完全颠倒了新化学品审查流程。EPA在其对新化学品的最基本义务上失职，即保护公众免受不合理风险。”此外，这两种光酸产生剂似乎还属于PFAS（全氟和多氟烷基物质），即常被称为“永久化学品”的合成化合物。它们具有异常牢固的化学键，即使在环境中暴露也能长期存续。

半导体行业历来是PFAS的使用大户，研究人员正努力寻找清理这些芯片制造化学品的途径。在没有法规强制要求从排放物中去除这些新化学品的情况下，批准其使用可能对环境造成灾难性影响。类似的担忧也出现在针对美光（Micron）纽约新工厂的诉讼中——诉讼称该公司获得的废水与空气许可仍可能让这些“永久化学品”泄漏到奥奈达河。环保组织承认，美国本土芯片生产确实需要使用这些潜在有害化学品，但EPA必须确保它们不会进入水系统，并保障相关工作人员免受接触危害。

当前美国政府正大力推动半导体制造回流，总统唐纳德·特朗普去年曾签署行政令，以加快数据中心所需化学品的审批流程。这两个新化学品是否与该行政令直接相关尚不明确，但这一事件凸显了产业扩张与公共健康、环境保护之间的尖锐矛盾。在AI浪潮下，数据中心对芯片的需求激增，而如何在满足产业需求的同时，防止有毒化学品对人类和环境造成不可逆的伤害，成为监管机构亟待解决的难题。

items.title: Nvidia to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, report claims — could strengthen Nvidia's open-model strategy and shore up position against rivals
items.description: Nvidia reportedly plans to buy Hugging Face at a price that exceeds its revenue by over 80 times, making it a major strategic investment in AI ecosystem.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 2 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, according to The Information, citing a person familiar with the deal. If the report is accurate and Nvidia indeed buys Hugging Face, the purchase could strengthen Nvidia's open-model strategy, provide another route to sell AI hardware, and help defend its hardware business as Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other major hyperscalers develop their own accelerators.Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft)The data center cooling state of playThe custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the priceGTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this yearDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleNvidia sells hundreds of billions worth of AI hardware every year. Although the ubiquity of its CUDA software stack and leading performance of its hardware are the primary reasons why Nvidia's AI platforms are sold like hot cakes, another important factor is that many AI models were trained on Nvidia hardware and are optimized to run on it. Therefore, the more models trained on Nvidia hardware, the more products the company is going to sell eventually.Hugging Face is an AI development platform best known for the Hugging Face Hub, a GitHub-like repository where researchers and developers publish, discover, download, and collaborate on AI models, datasets, and applications. Hugging Face also develops widely used software such as the Transformers library and provides tools and cloud services for training, optimizing, and deploying models on different types of AI hardware.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: In addition to hosting models, datasets, and applications, Hugging Face provides software that helps developers optimize and deploy AI models on different CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators, while its Inference Endpoints service lets customers run models on managed infrastructure hosted by AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.To make things simple, Inference Endpoints allows customers to select the provider, region, hardware type, and instance. What is important here is that the hardware used by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft is not all Nvidia. Hugging Face currently offers, depending on the provider, AWS Inferentia, AMD Instinct, Google TPU, Intel CPUs, and Nvidia accelerators, among other configurations. You may like Nvidia teams up with financial giants to create $500 billion AI infrastructure funds Nvidia revenue tops $96 billion as memory commitments soar to $160 billion Nvidia and SK Group enter $500 billion AI partnership OpenAI models, datasets, popular applications, and abilities to optimize and deploy AI models on different hardware make Hugging Face strategically important to Nvidia. On the one hand, the company can make the platform exclusively rely on its hardware, though this may face a backlash from the community, so this is something unlikely to happen in the short term (even assuming Nvidia is indeed set to buy Hugging Face). On the other hand, Nvidia wants open models to remain competitive with proprietary offerings from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI that may eventually get optimized for proprietary non-Nvidia hardware. Nvidia has been building its own Nemotron open models and has committed tens of billions of dollars to the effort. Furthermore, as Hugging Face grows, so is adoption of AI hardware in general and Nvidia hardware in particular.Hugging Face is growing rapidly, but its revenue remains modest compared with the purchase price, according to The Information. The 10-year-old company recently reached approximately $150 million in annualized revenue, compared with about $100 million several months earlier, which puts Nvidia's price at roughly 80 times forward revenue, something that clearly highlights the strategic nature of the acquisition. Negotiations reportedly began after Hugging Face received acquisition interest elsewhere.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsCEO and co-founder Clem Delangue said in June that paying subscribers doubled during the first half of 2026 and recently said the company was close to profitability. Demand has benefited from improving Chinese open models from Z.ai, Moonshot, and DeepSeek.If Nvidia proceeds with the takeover, the transaction will be a part of Nvidia's increasingly aggressive investments across the AI ecosystem that spans from hardware to models to software. Last week, Nvidia agreed to pay $6 billion to license development technology from open-model developer Poolside and offered jobs to more than 100 employees. Nvidia also acquired Groq, Enfabrica, Essential AI, Illumex, and Kumo AI, just to name some. items.titleZh: 英伟达拟以129亿美元收购Hugging Face，报道称——此举或强化其开放模型战略并巩固对竞争对手的优势
items.descriptionZh:
英伟达（Nvidia）据传已同意以129亿美元收购人工智能开发平台Hugging Face。这一消息由The Information援引知情人士报道，如果交易属实，将标志着英伟达在AI生态领域迄今最大规模的并购之一，其战略意义远超单纯的技术或人才收购。

英伟达每年售出价值数千亿美元的AI硬件。其CUDA软件生态的普及性和硬件性能的领先地位固然是核心驱动力，但另一个不容忽视的因素是：大量AI模型都是在英伟达硬件上完成训练并针对其架构优化的。这意味着，在英伟达平台上训练的模型越多，英伟达最终卖出的产品就越多。Hugging Face恰好是全球最大的AI模型开源社区，其Hub平台如同AI领域的GitHub，研究人员和开发者在这里发布、发现、下载并协作开发各类AI模型、数据集和应用。此外，Hugging Face还开发了广受欢迎的Transformers库，并提供跨不同AI硬件类型的训练、优化和部署工具及云服务。

Hugging Face的Inference Endpoints服务值得特别关注：它允许客户自由选择云服务提供商、区域、硬件类型和实例配置。关键在于，亚马逊、谷歌和微软所用的硬件并非全部来自英伟达——目前该平台根据服务商不同，支持AWS Inferentia、AMD Instinct、谷歌TPU、英特尔CPU以及英伟达加速器等多种配置。这种硬件中立性恰恰突显了此次收购的战略敏感性。

对英伟达而言，Hugging Face的战略价值体现在多个层面。一方面，英伟达理论上可以让该平台独家依赖自家硬件，但这可能引发开源社区的强烈反弹，短期内大概率不会发生。另一方面，英伟达希望开源模型能够持续与Anthropic、OpenAI等公司的闭源模型竞争——后者可能会针对非英伟达的定制加速器进行优化。为此，英伟达一直在打造自己的Nemotron开源模型体系，并已投入数百亿美元。同时，随着Hugging Face社区的成长，整个AI硬件市场的规模也在扩大，英伟达作为市场领导者自然受益最大。

从财务数据看，这家成立十年的公司增长迅猛：其年化收入已从几个月前的约1亿美元攀升至约1.5亿美元，但相对于129亿美元的收购价仍显规模有限——这意味着估值约为远期收入的80倍，充分体现了这笔交易的战略性而非财务性。据报道，谈判始于Hugging Face收到其他方的收购意向之后。公司CEO兼联合创始人Clem Delangue在6月表示，2026年上半年付费订阅用户数翻了一番，公司已接近盈利。需求增长部分受益于Z.ai、Moonshot和DeepSeek等中国开源模型的质量提升。

值得注意的是，这并非英伟达近期唯一的激进投资。就在上周，英伟达同意支付60亿美元从开源模型开发商Poolside获得开发技术许可，并向其100多名员工提供工作机会。此外，英伟达还接连收购了Groq、Enfabrica、Essential AI、Illumex和Kumo AI等多家AI公司。

如果Hugging Face收购最终落地，这笔交易将成为英伟达在AI领域从硬件到模型再到软件全栈布局中的关键一环，也将对整个AI开源生态的走向产生深远影响。

items.title: Hot Chips 2026: OpenAI's Jalapeño AI ASIC unpacked — accelerator developed using AI achieves efficiency and throughput gains against power-hungry Blackwell
items.description: OpenAI's first AI accelerator fails to beat Nvidia's Blackwell in terms of raw performance, but it can offer very good performance-per-watt and low latency, which is exactly what the doctor ordered for inference workloads.
items.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter OpenAI made quite a splash back in June, when it unveiled its 'Jalapeño' AI accelerator and revealed that the chip reached tape-out in just nine months. At the Hot Chips conference, OpenAI disclosed more details about the architecture of its Jalapeño inference processor as well as shared its target and real-world performance numbers. The company claims its NUMA-style spatial architecture enables Jalapeño to outperform Nvidia's GB200 and GB300 in low-latency inference and in terms of performance-per-watt, while a 2,048-processor system scales to 27 exaFLOPS and 32 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth. (Image credit: OpenAI)A massive chip with massive scalingOpenAI's Jalapeño is a massive AI inference accelerator co-developed with Broadcom, with 216 GB of HBM4 memory and up to 15.4 TB/s of bandwidth. The processor delivers up to 3.4 MXFP8 PFLOPS as well as up to 13.4 MXFP4 PFLOPS at 700W, which makes it suitable for inference, though the MXFP4 format may not be enough for training. The ASIC has a 700W power rating and operates at 1.70 GHz on silicon already running in OpenAI's labs, though OpenAI's engineers said at Hot Chips that the plan is to increase clocks up to 1.80 GHz, perhaps to get higher peak performance. (Image credit: OpenAI)On the scalability side of matters, Jalapeño can scale to 128 accelerators in a local rack interconnected using Ethernet at 600 GB/s and to 2,048 ASICs in a 16-rack pod configuration at 200 GB/s per processor. The complete system offers 27 EFLOPS of MXFP4 performance, 432 TB of HBM4 memory, and 32 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth. For connectivity, OpenAI uses Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Ethernet switches and what it calls a 'half-flattened' two-level Clos topology that provides higher bandwidth for tensor-parallel traffic, lower bandwidth for expert-parallel communication, and prioritizes low latency for both. During the Q&A session, OpenAI confirmed that the scale-up network uses Ethernet with 200-Gb/s links. Jalapeño's physical hardware around the Broadcom-made chip is set to be made by Celestica.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: On paper, Jalapeño's specifications look good, but they barely look impressive compared to Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra accelerators (10 FP8 PFLOPS, 20/15 sparse/dense NVFP4 PFLOPS). However, OpenAI argues that raw compute and memory bandwidth are not what makes its Jalapeño platform different.The company says a 128-ASIC Jalapeño domain has more than 1 PB/s of aggregate HBM4 bandwidth, which is significantly higher compared to GB300 NVL72 (576 TB/s). A one-trillion-parameter model using FP4 weights requires about 0.5 TB. So, purely from a bandwidth perspective, the system could read the entire model more than 2,000 times per second. Meanwhile, actual inference performance comes nowhere near that theoretical ceiling, which is why hardware developers do not tend to add HBM bandwidth infinitely. You may like OpenAI’s 700W Jalapeño ASIC outpaces 1,400W Nvidia flagship GPU Broadcom and OpenAI unveil custom-built Jalapeño inference processor Hot Chips 2026: Intel dives deep on Crescent Island AI accelerator Smart data movementInstead, Jalapeño uses what OpenAI describes as a memory-sliced, or NUMA-style, architecture. The chip has 64 core slices, and each of them is paired with its own HBM slice to guarantee predictable latency and bandwidth. OpenAI says this arrangement avoids conflicts associated with a unified memory subsystem and lets frequently used operands remain close to the compute resources that need them. OpenAI does not explain why it chose exactly 64 slices, which likely means it was a sweet spot for the current architecture. (Image credit: OpenAI)To connect the 64 core slices, OpenAI uses a specialized high-bandwidth, low-latency collective network that moves data coupled to compute operations 'register-to-register, with zero conflicts' in a bid to eliminate several performance bottlenecks. In addition, Jalapeño has a separate general-purpose network-on-chip (NoC) that handles less common communication (e.g., remote/global memory accesses) and provides access to the external scale-up network.The distinction between these fabrics is substantial. OpenAI describes the general NoC as deliberately more 'anemic than you would expect from a normal chip architecture' as it does not want performance-critical traffic to use it typically. By contrast, the ultra-fast collective network organizes data movement, so operands arrive in registers when needed rather than leaving compute engines and then waiting for memory, network traffic, or global synchronization, which creates internal performance bottlenecks.In general, it looks like one network is optimized for speed and predictability for inter-core communications, whereas the other is optimized for general use cases. Trying to make one NoC do both would require a much more capable general network, consume more silicon/power, and reintroduce contention.A different approachOpenAI's Jalapeño is also designed for the very different types of work that happen during a single agentic inference request. What to read next Anthropic co-designing custom AI inference chips to bypass costly Nvidia GPUs Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia presents Groq 3 LPX architecture and unveils its first third-party inference benchmark AMD takes the wraps off its Instinct MI455X AI accelerator To explain how it works, let us compare OpenAI's and Nvidia's approaches. Nvidia's standard system-level decomposition is primarily two phases: prefill and decode. Prefill is generally compute-bound (which is why Nvidia tried to assign Rubin CPX with GDDR7 for this one), while decode is generally memory-bound (which is why Nvidia wants to keep GPUs with HBM for this). By contrast, OpenAI breaks the process into three phases: prefill (compute-bound), draft (latency-bound), and verification (bandwidth-bound). (Image credit: OpenAI)In theory, OpenAI could have assigned each phase to a different type of specialized accelerator. However, the amount of prefill, drafting, and verification changes depending on the model, context length, token efficiency, and software algorithms. As a result, it is hard to predict the number of processors that must be deployed, so it's inevitable that some phases would sit idle. To that end, it makes more sense to develop one balanced ASIC that can do everything.As a bonus, a universal inference accelerator does not need to move increasingly large KV cache to its peers, unlike highly specialized ASICs, which ultimately means less power consumed.Chips develop chipsDespite Jalapeño's exceptionally short development cycle, OpenAI says that most of the processor was designed from scratch rather than assembled from existing Broadcom accelerator IP. OpenAI's Richard Ho said the compute die reuses some interface IP, but most of its Register Transfer Level (RTL) was newly written using XLS and Verilog. Meanwhile, development moved remarkably quickly: initial RTL work began in February 2025, the design taped out in November, first silicon arrived in May 2026, and OpenAI had Codex running on Jalapeño that same month. (Image credit: OpenAI)One reason OpenAI was able to move so fast with its development was its extensive use of AI to assist and optimize the design. More than half of the core was written using the XLS hardware language and compiler infrastructure, while OpenAI's own AI models searched for ways to improve power, performance, and area (PPA). Compared with human 'baseline' designs, OpenAI reports improvements of 56% for a BF16 multiplier, 21% for an FP4 dot-product block, and 10% for an FP32 accumulator, along with 10% and 8% area reductions for the matrix and SIMD units. The company says that AI-assisted optimization even helped squeeze circuitry into a floorplan block that otherwise would not have fit, though OpenAI remains tight-lipped about what circuitry it was. (Image credit: OpenAI)Jalapeño is OpenAI's first, but not the last, attempt to develop custom inference hardware. The company says its 2nd Generation already well into development and heading toward tape out, while Richard Ho said during the presentation that Gen 3 is already 'operational,' even though his slide said 'planned.'ProgrammabilityBecause Jalapeño features its unique spatial and sliced architecture, it is programmed differently from Nvidia's CUDA GPUs. OpenAI says Jalapeño can be programmed using a low-level programming environment in the open-source Triton ecosystem. Unlike the latest versions of CUDA, which ensure that its code runs on all Nvidia GPUs and aligns with the tensor-heavy execution model of Blackwell processors and their successors, Jalapeño gives software more explicit control over where data and computation are placed.Each core has fast access to its local portion of HBM; these cores are interconnected using an ultra-fast network, so the software must be able to determine where tensors are physically located and how they are distributed across the chip. This makes programming the spatial architecture more complicated, so OpenAI also uses AI to find efficient data placement, scheduling, and communication patterns and to optimize kernels for the hardware.Meanwhile, optimal mapping is architecture-dependent, so once OpenAI changes the number of cores, local-memory organization, collective-network topology/bandwidth, or compute resources in next generations of its accelerators, the old placement and scheduling may no longer be optimal and will require AI tools to perform hardware-specific optimizations again. By contrast, software written for Blackwell will work on Rubin and then Feynman without modifications.But how good is OpenAI's software stack compared to CUDA? Apparently, good enough, based on performance results published by the company.PerformanceInstead of comparing peak performance numbers, OpenAI used SemiAnalysis' InferenceX benchmark to compare Jalapeño and Nvidia's GB200/GB300 across their complete latency-versus-throughput curves. The company measured how many tokens each system could deliver at comparable user-perceived latency and normalized the results by package power — 700W for Jalapeño, 1,200W for GB200, and 1,400W for GB300 — meaning that while Nvidia's hardware can lead in terms of absolute performance, OpenAI's accelerator leads in efficiency. Image 1 of 9 (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) (Image credit: OpenAI) Image 1 of 9 View Original Image 2 of 9 View Original Image 3 of 9 View Original Image 4 of 9 View Original Image 5 of 9 View Original Image 6 of 9 View Original Image 7 of 9 View Original Image 8 of 9 View Original Image 9 of 9 View Original Compared to Nvidia GB200/GB300, Jalapeño delivers:Roughly 1.5X – 1.9X higher peak throughput per watt1.7X – 3.6X lower end-to-end latency2.1X – 4.1X lower minimum time between tokens (TBT)At Nvidia's minimum-TBT operating points, Jalapeño can deliver up to 104.3X higher throughput. This methodology particularly favors Jalapeño's strength at low latency, so the result is significantly inflated. The 104.3X figure means that at GB300's lowest-latency operating point, Jalapeño can maintain 104.3X higher throughput, not that Jalapeño is 104.3X faster overall.OpenAI also noted that its internal models show an even larger advantage for the Jalapeño platform and says applying multi-token prediction to Jalapeño can improve latency by another 3X to 5X at equivalent efficiency.AI makes chips nowOpenAI used Hot Chips 2026 to fully detail Jalapeño, its first custom inference AI accelerator co-developed with Broadcom. The ASIC relies on a NUMA-style architecture built around 64 memory/core slices, carries 216 GB of HBM4 memory, and has compute performance of up 13.4 MXFP4 PFLOPS at 700W. Being aimed at AI data centers, Jalapeño scales from 128 accelerators per rack to 2,048 inference processor per pod and can provided up to 27 EFLOPS of MXFP4 compute, 432 TB of HBM4, and 32 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth per cluster.While absolute performance of Jalapeño may fall short of what Nvidia's Blackwell or Rubin offer, the company argues that the main advantage of its AI inference accelerator platform is its performance-per-watt achievements as well low latency. OpenAI says its Jalapeño delivers roughly 1.5X – 1.9X higher peak peak-performance-per watt and 1.7X – 3.6X lower end-to-end latency than Nvidia GB200/GB300 in its InferenceX comparisons.Perhaps the most impressive, or maybe even terrifying, though certainly not unexpected thing that OpenAI revealed is that AI played a major role in Jalapeño's unusually fast nine-month RTL-to-tapeout development cycle and also enabled the company to improve performance, power, and area, of the design. Jalapeño's successor is already heading toward tapeout and OpenAI's 3rd Generation AI accelerator is already in development. items.titleZh: Hot Chips 2026: OpenAI's Jalapeño AI ASIC unpacked — accelerator developed using AI achieves efficiency and throughput gains against power-hungry Blackwell
items.descriptionZh:
今年六月，OpenAI发布了与博通联合开发的定制AI推理加速器“Jalapeño”，并宣布芯片在短短九个月内便完成流片（tape-out），在业界引发广泛关注。在刚刚举行的Hot Chips 2026大会上，OpenAI进一步披露了这颗芯片的架构细节、实测性能数据以及背后的设计哲学，其中最引人注目的是：OpenAI声称Jalapeño在低延迟推理和能效比方面均优于Nvidia的GB200和GB300平台，同时一套由2048颗处理器组成的系统可扩展至27 exaFLOPS的算力和32 PB/s的聚合内存带宽。

从物理规格来看，Jalapeño是一颗规模庞大的AI推理专用芯片。它集成了216 GB的HBM4内存，提供高达15.4 TB/s的带宽；在700W功耗下，可输出最高3.4 MXFP8 PFLOPS（每秒千万亿次浮点运算）和13.4 MXFP4 PFLOPS的算力，显然是为推理场景而生——MXFP4精度对训练任务可能仍不够。芯片在OpenAI实验室已实际运行的硅片上运行频率为1.70 GHz，工程师表示计划将频率提升至1.80 GHz以进一步挖掘峰值性能。

在扩展性设计上，Jalapeño采用以太网互连：本地机架内最多可部署128颗加速器，每颗获得600 GB/s互连带宽；而一个由16个机架组成的Pod可容纳2048颗ASIC，每颗带宽为200 GB/s。整个系统的理论峰值可达27 EFLOPS（MXFP4精度）、432 TB HBM4总容量和32 PB/s聚合内存带宽。网络层面，OpenAI使用博通Tomahawk 6以太网交换芯片，并采用其称为“半扁平化”（half-flattened）的两级Clos拓扑——该拓扑为张量并行流量提供更高带宽，为专家并行通信分配较低带宽，同时对两者都优先保障低延迟。在会议问答环节，OpenAI确认其scale-up网络采用200 Gb/s以太网链路。物理硬件（围绕博通芯片展开的板卡等）由Celestica代工。

纸面参数固然亮眼，但相比Nvidia Blackwell Ultra（FP8为10 PFLOPS，NVFP4稀疏/密集为20/15 PFLOPS），Jalapeño的绝对算力并不突出。OpenAI强调，其平台的差异化优势不在原始算力或内存带宽，而在于架构设计。一个由128颗ASIC组成的Jalapeño域，聚合HBM4带宽超过1 PB/s，而Nvidia GB300 NVL72的带宽为576 TB/s。一个一万亿参数、FP4权重的模型大约需要0.5 TB存储，因此从纯带宽角度看，该系统理论上每秒钟可将整个模型读取超过2000次——但实际推理性能远达不到这一理论天花板，这也是硬件开发者不会无限堆加HBM带宽的原因。

Jalapeño的真正创新在于其“内存切片式”或NUMA风格的空间架构。芯片包含64个核心切片，每个切片都配有独立的HBM内存切片，从而保证延迟和带宽的高度可预测。OpenAI表示，这种设计避免了统一内存子系统带来的冲突，并使频繁使用的操作数能够保留在需要它们的计算资源附近。至于为何选择64个切片，OpenAI并未解释，大概率是在当前架构下的一个最佳平衡点。

连接64个核心切片的是OpenAI专门设计的高带宽、低延迟集合通信网络。该网络将数据移动与计算操作紧密耦合，实现“寄存器到寄存器、零冲突”的数据传输，消除了多个性能瓶颈。此外，Jalapeño还设有一个独立的通用片上网络（NoC），负责处理不常见的通信（如远程或全局内存访问），并提供对外部规模扩展网络的接入。OpenAI刻意将通用NoC设计得“比正常芯片架构预期的要弱”，因为不希望性能关键的流量走这条路。两种网络分工明确：一个是针对核间通信的速度和可预测性优化，另一个是针对通用场景优化。如果试图让一个NoC同时承担两种职责，将需要更强大的通用网络，消耗更多芯片面积和功耗，并重新引入资源竞争。

Jalapeño的另一大创新是针对“agentic推理”过程中不同阶段的工作负载特点重新定义了任务分解。Nvidia的标准分解为两个阶段：prefill（预填充，计算密集）和decode（解码，内存密集）。OpenAI则将其拆分为三个阶段：prefill（计算密集）、draft（草稿生成，延迟敏感）和verification（验证，带宽密集）。理论上可以为每个阶段配备不同种类的专用加速器，但prefill、draft和verification的比例会随模型、上下文长度、token效率及软件算法变化，很难预测需要部署的处理器数量，必然导致部分阶段闲置。因此，开发一颗能够兼顾所有任务的平衡型ASIC更为合理。此外，通用推理加速器无需像高度专用ASIC那样在不同处理器间搬运不断增长的KV缓存，这最终也降低了功耗。

Jalapeño的开发周期短得惊人，而OpenAI表示，这颗芯片的大部分设计是从零开始，而非直接复用博通现有的加速器IP。OpenAI的Richard Ho透露，计算die复用了一些接口IP，但绝大多数寄存器传输级（RTL）代码是使用XLS和Verilog新编写的。开发时间线极其紧凑：RTL工作始于2025年2月，同年11月流片，2026年5月拿到首批硅片，并在当月让Codex模型在Jalapeño上运行起来。

如此快的速度，很大程度上得益于AI辅助设计。Jalapeño的核心超过一半是使用XLS硬件语言和编译器基础设施编写的，而OpenAI自己的AI模型则被用来搜索改进功耗、性能和面积（PPA）的机会。与人类“基线”设计相比，AI优化的BF16乘法器性能提升56%，FP4点积模块提升21%，FP32累加器提升10%，矩阵和SIMD单元面积分别缩减10%和8%。OpenAI还提到，AI辅助优化成功将一些电路“挤”进原本无法容纳的布局块中，但未透露具体是何种电路。

由于Jalapeño采用独特的空间切片架构，它的编程方式与Nvidia CUDA GPU截然不同。OpenAI表示，Jalapeño可以通过开源Triton生态中的低级编程环境进行编程。与确保代码在所有Nvidia GPU上运行、并顺应Blackwell及后续处理器张量密集型执行模型的CUDA不同，Jalapeño让软件更直接地控制数据和计算的放置位置。每个核心都能快速访问其本地HBM部分，核心间通过超快网络互连，因此软件必须确定张量在芯片上的物理位置及分布方式。这使空间架构的编程变得更为复杂，OpenAI因此也使用AI来寻找高效的数据放置、调度和通信模式，并为硬件优化内核。

然而，这种优化映射高度依赖具体架构——一旦OpenAI在下一代加速器中改变核心数量、本地内存组织、集合网络拓扑/带宽或计算资源，旧有的放置和调度策略可能不再最优，需要再次借助AI工具进行硬件专属优化。相比之下，为Blackwell编写的软件可以在Rubin甚至Feynman上无需修改运行。那么OpenAI的软件栈与CUDA相比表现如何？从其公布的性能结果来看，至少已经足够好。

性能方面，OpenAI没有简单对比峰值数字，而是采用SemiAnalysis的InferenceX基准，将Jalapeño与Nvidia GB200/GB300放在完整的延迟-吞吐量曲线上进行对比。他们测量了在相近“可感知”延迟下各系统能输出多少token，再按封装功耗（Jalapeño 700W、GB200 1200W、GB300 1400W）进行归一化——这意味着Nvidia硬件可能在绝对性能上领先，但OpenAI加速器在效率上胜出。结果显示：
- 峰值吞吐量/功率比GB200/GB300高出约1.5倍至1.9倍；
- 端到端延迟低1.7倍至3.6倍；
- 最小token间隔（TBT）低2.1倍至4.1倍；
- 在Nvidia最小TBT工作点上，Jalapeño可提供高达104.3倍的吞吐量。不过需要注意，这一数字高度偏向Jalapeño的优势领域——低延迟，因此存在明显放大效果，并不代表Jalapeño整体快104.3倍。

OpenAI还表示，其内部模型显示出Jalapeño平台更大的优势，并且利用多token预测技术（multi-token prediction）在同等效率下可将延迟再降低3至5倍。

总而言之，OpenAI在Hot Chips 2026上全面展示了Jalapeño——这是其与博通共同打造的首款定制推理AI加速器。该ASIC采用围绕64个内存/核心切片的NUMA风格架构，配备216 GB HBM4，在700W功耗下提供高达13.4 MXFP4 PFLOPS的计算性能。面向AI数据中心，Jalapeño从单机架128颗加速器扩展到单Pod 2048颗推理处理器，可提供27 EFLOPS的MXFP4算力、432 TB HBM4内存和32 PB/s的集群聚合内存带宽。虽然绝对性能可能不及Nvidia Blackwell或Rubin，但OpenAI主张其AI推理加速器平台的核心优势在于每瓦性能和低延迟——在InferenceX对比中，Jalapeño的每瓦峰值性能比Nvidia GB200/GB300高出约1.5至1.9倍，端到端延迟低1.7至3.6倍。

或许最令人印象深刻（甚至令人震撼）、但也在意料之中的是：AI在Jalapeño仅九个月的RTL到流片开发周期中扮演了关键角色，并帮助改善了设计的性能、功耗和面积。Jalapeño的继任者第二代芯片已接近流片，而第三代加速器也已进入开发阶段。AI不仅是在芯片上运行的工作负载，如今也在成为设计芯片本身的强大工具，这或许正预示着半导体行业未来的新常态。

items.title: When agents act on their own, governance has to live in the data layer
items.description:
Presented by EDB 

As enterprises give AI agents more autonomy — the ability to plan, decide, and act across systems without a human approving each step — a hard question moves to the center of every architecture review: When an agent tries to complete an action that it was never authorized to do, what actually stops it?
These are your agents, running on your models, touching your data in your infrastructure — and the responsibility for what they do sits with you. That responsibility can’t be met in hindsight or with a set of abstract policies that live on paper but not in practice. Agents need rules in the context of the moment, because they don’t exercise overriding judgment of their own actions.
Consider a simple rule: Never open the car door. Followed literally, an agent could never get in or out of the car at all. But if you change the context (the car has just crashed, there’s a fire, someone is hurt and needs to get out), then the rule you actually want is the opposite. Context in the moment is everything. We are asking agents to do intelligent things; that requires intelligent rules.
The instinct is to add guardrails around the agent: instructions, policies, and monitoring layered above the model. Those mechanisms matter, but they share a structural limit: The car-door rule is plausible right up until the moment you actually have to decide whether to open the door. Controls at the agent layer are only as reliable as the agent’s output is predictable, and autonomy is precisely the property that makes that output hard to predict. Governance that depends on reviewing an action before it happens cannot keep pace with a system that acts in milliseconds, across many systems at once.
Governance has to become executable, and enforced where agents actually do their work: at the operational data layer, in the context, and exactly at the moment it is happening. 
The data layer is the enforcement point
Agents create value by touching data. They query it, retrieve it, transform it, and increasingly act on it. A policy that says an agent should not reach a certain class of data is meaningful only if the system can deny that access at the moment the agent requests it. Additionally, a principle that says AI must be auditable is meaningful only if the organization can reconstruct what the agent did, what data it touched, which user it acted for, and what resulted. When governance lives at the data layer, it holds regardless of how the agent was built or how it behaves, because the control is a property of the database itself, not a promise made by the agent.
Agent behavior may be probabilistic. Governance cannot be
The enterprise should not rely on a model choosing to follow policy. The policy has to be enforced by the system. That is the difference between hoping an actor stays in bounds and constructing bounds it cannot cross to begin with.
The controls that make this real are ones many enterprises already run at the data layer: role- and attribute-based access, row- and column-level security, classification and masking, policy as code, and complete audit trails. 
What agents change is not the mechanism, but who the mechanism has to recognize. Identity management has to treat the agent as a principal in its own right, with its own identity and a purpose declared when the session opens. 
Once purpose is bound to identity, the policy engine can evaluate it the same way it evaluates role or department today, and the record of what happened can capture not just who acted and what they touched, but what they declared they were there to do.
In practice, this resolves into nine controls, grouped under three imperatives:
Enforce it

Role- and attribute-based access control enforced at query time, for agents as well as users

Dynamic column masking driven by the same policy path

Agent identity as a first-class principal, with declared purpose bound at session start and the acting user preserved

See it and prove it

Classification and tagging that drives policy

Session-level audit logging that records which agent acted, for which user, and under what declared purpose

Lineage across pipelines, so a result can be traced back to the request that produced it

Unify and harden

Centralized, portable policy management

Encryption at rest and in transit

Consistent enforcement across on-prem, cloud, and sovereign or air-gapped environments

“Declared purpose is what makes the difference. It becomes an attribute the access layer already understands, evaluated in the same policy path as role and row-level security. The enforcement mechanism does not change. What changes is that the agent's purpose is part of what it evaluates, and part of what the record proves afterward,” says Priyanka Jain, VP, product management, data & AI governance, EDB. 
Wherever you are in your AI adoption journey, enforcement at the data layer is what lets you move faster rather than slower. The controls are already in the database. The difference is that agents now have to pass through them.
A digital leash, not a locked door
The goal is not to stop agents from doing useful work. It is to define how far an agent can go, what it can touch, what it can change, what requires escalation, and how the organization can reconstruct events if something goes wrong. Governed this way, agents are identified, scoped, monitored, and auditable. The enterprise can adopt them faster, because security, risk, and leadership teams trust the operating model underneath.
Open, sovereign, and enforceable at the source
Built on open source Postgres, this open foundation keeps enterprises in control of where their data lives, who can reach it, and under what policy, without ceding governance to a layer they don’t own or can’t inspect. For regulated industries, that combination of data sovereignty and source-level enforcement isn’t a nice-to-have; it’s the precondition for putting agents into production at all.

items.content:
Presented by EDB

As enterprises give AI agents more autonomy — the ability to plan, decide, and act across systems without a human approving each step — a hard question moves to the center of every architecture review: When an agent tries to complete an action that it was never authorized to do, what actually stops it?

These are your agents, running on your models, touching your data in your infrastructure — and the responsibility for what they do sits with you. That responsibility can’t be met in hindsight or with a set of abstract policies that live on paper but not in practice. Agents need rules in the context of the moment, because they don’t exercise overriding judgment of their own actions.

Consider a simple rule: Never open the car door. Followed literally, an agent could never get in or out of the car at all. But if you change the context (the car has just crashed, there’s a fire, someone is hurt and needs to get out), then the rule you actually want is the opposite. Context in the moment is everything. We are asking agents to do intelligent things; that requires intelligent rules.

The instinct is to add guardrails around the agent: instructions, policies, and monitoring layered above the model. Those mechanisms matter, but they share a structural limit: The car-door rule is plausible right up until the moment you actually have to decide whether to open the door. Controls at the agent layer are only as reliable as the agent’s output is predictable, and autonomy is precisely the property that makes that output hard to predict. Governance that depends on reviewing an action before it happens cannot keep pace with a system that acts in milliseconds, across many systems at once.

Governance has to become executable, and enforced where agents actually do their work: at the operational data layer, in the context, and exactly at the moment it is happening.

The data layer is the enforcement point

Agents create value by touching data. They query it, retrieve it, transform it, and increasingly act on it. A policy that says an agent should not reach a certain class of data is meaningful only if the system can deny that access at the moment the agent requests it. Additionally, a principle that says AI must be auditable is meaningful only if the organization can reconstruct what the agent did, what data it touched, which user it acted for, and what resulted. When governance lives at the data layer, it holds regardless of how the agent was built or how it behaves, because the control is a property of the database itself, not a promise made by the agent.

Agent behavior may be probabilistic. Governance cannot be

The enterprise should not rely on a model choosing to follow policy. The policy has to be enforced by the system. That is the difference between hoping an actor stays in bounds and constructing bounds it cannot cross to begin with.

The controls that make this real are ones many enterprises already run at the data layer: role- and attribute-based access, row- and column-level security, classification and masking, policy as code, and complete audit trails.

What agents change is not the mechanism, but who the mechanism has to recognize. Identity management has to treat the agent as a principal in its own right, with its own identity and a purpose declared when the session opens.

Once purpose is bound to identity, the policy engine can evaluate it the same way it evaluates role or department today, and the record of what happened can capture not just who acted and what they touched, but what they declared they were there to do.

In practice, this resolves into nine controls, grouped under three imperatives:

Enforce it

  • Role- and attribute-based access control enforced at query time, for agents as well as users

  • Dynamic column masking driven by the same policy path

  • Agent identity as a first-class principal, with declared purpose bound at session start and the acting user preserved

See it and prove it

  • Classification and tagging that drives policy

  • Session-level audit logging that records which agent acted, for which user, and under what declared purpose

  • Lineage across pipelines, so a result can be traced back to the request that produced it

Unify and harden

  • Centralized, portable policy management

  • Encryption at rest and in transit

  • Consistent enforcement across on-prem, cloud, and sovereign or air-gapped environments

“Declared purpose is what makes the difference. It becomes an attribute the access layer already understands, evaluated in the same policy path as role and row-level security. The enforcement mechanism does not change. What changes is that the agent's purpose is part of what it evaluates, and part of what the record proves afterward,” says Priyanka Jain, VP, product management, data & AI governance, EDB.

Wherever you are in your AI adoption journey, enforcement at the data layer is what lets you move faster rather than slower. The controls are already in the database. The difference is that agents now have to pass through them.

A digital leash, not a locked door

The goal is not to stop agents from doing useful work. It is to define how far an agent can go, what it can touch, what it can change, what requires escalation, and how the organization can reconstruct events if something goes wrong. Governed this way, agents are identified, scoped, monitored, and auditable. The enterprise can adopt them faster, because security, risk, and leadership teams trust the operating model underneath.

Open, sovereign, and enforceable at the source

Built on open source Postgres, this open foundation keeps enterprises in control of where their data lives, who can reach it, and under what policy, without ceding governance to a layer they don’t own or can’t inspect. For regulated industries, that combination of data sovereignty and source-level enforcement isn’t a nice-to-have; it’s the precondition for putting agents into production at all.

Agentic systems will keep getting more capable and more autonomous. That is a reason to be deliberate about where control lives, not a reason to slow down. The enterprises that enforce governance at the data layer can move aggressively on AI, because the thing protecting their data is more than just wishful thinking.

items.titleZh: When agents act on their own, governance has to live in the data layer
items.descriptionZh:
随着企业赋予AI代理越来越多的自主权——让它们能够跨系统规划、决策和执行操作，而无须人工逐步审批——一个尖锐的问题成为了所有架构评审的焦点：当代理试图执行一个从未被授权完成的动作时，究竟是什么机制能真正阻止它？这些代理运行在你的模型之上，触达你的数据，栖身于你的基础设施之中，它们的行为后果最终由你承担。这种责任无法靠事后追溯来履行，也无法靠一套只停留在纸面上、从未在现实中落地的抽象政策来兑现。代理需要的是在当下情境中的规则，因为它们自身并不会对自己行为的高下做出超越性的判断。

考虑一条简单规则：永远不要打开车门。如果机械地遵守，代理将永远无法上下车。但若情境改变（车刚发生碰撞、起火、有人受伤需要逃生），你真正想要的规则恰好相反。当下情境决定一切。我们要求代理做出智能行为，就需要智能的规则。

直觉上，人们倾向于在代理周围加装护栏：在模型之上堆叠指令、策略和监控。这些机制固然重要，但它们共享同一个结构性局限：车门规则在真正需要决定是否开门之前，看上去总是合理的。代理层面的控制，其可靠性完全取决于代理输出的可预测性，而自主性恰恰是让输出变得难以预测的根源。依赖于在行动发生前审查的治理方式，无法跟上毫秒级、跨多系统并行运作的代理系统。

治理必须变得可执行，并且要在代理实际工作的地点强制执行——即操作数据层、在具体情境之中、在事件发生的当下。数据层才是执行点。代理通过触达数据创造价值：查询、检索、转换，并越来越多地直接作用于数据。一条“代理不应接触某类数据”的规则，只有在系统能在代理请求的那一刻拒绝访问时才有意义。同理，“AI必须可审计”的原则，只有在组织能完整还原代理做了什么、触达了哪些数据、代哪个用户行事、产生了什么结果时才成立。当治理落在数据层，无论代理如何构建、如何表现，它都始终成立，因为控制是数据库自身的属性，而非代理做出的承诺。

代理行为或许是概率性的，但治理绝不应该是概率性的。企业不应依赖模型“选择”去遵循策略；策略必须由系统强制执行。这正是“希望参与者在边界内行事”与“构筑其无法跨越的边界”之间的区别。

让这一切真正落地的控制机制，许多企业早就在数据层运行了：基于角色和属性的访问控制（RBAC/ABAC）、行级与列级安全、数据分类与脱敏、策略即代码（Policy as Code）、完整的审计追踪。代理改变的并非机制本身，而是机制必须识别的主体是谁。身份管理必须将代理视为一个独立的“主体”（principal），拥有自己的身份，并在会话开启时声明其“目的”（purpose）。一旦目的与身份绑定，策略引擎就能像今天评估角色或部门那样评估它；而事件记录不仅能捕捉到“谁操作了、触达了什么”，还能记录“他们声明自己来这里做什么”。

在实践中，这可以归结为九项控制，分属三个核心要求：

**强制执行**：在查询时对代理和用户同样实施基于角色/属性的访问控制；由同一策略路径驱动的动态列级脱敏；代理身份作为一等公民，在会话开始时绑定声明目的，同时保留真正的操作用户。

**可见与可证**：推动策略执行的分类与标签；会话级审计日志，记录是哪个代理、为哪个用户、在何种声明目的下操作；跨管线的数据血缘，使任何结果都能追溯至产生它的请求。

**统一与加固**：集中且可移植的策略管理；静态与传输中的加密；在本地、云端、主权或隔离环境中保持一致执行。

EDB数据与AI治理产品管理副总裁Priyanka Jain指出：“声明目的（declared purpose）是关键差异。它成为访问层已经理解的一个属性，与角色和行级安全在同一策略路径中被评估。执行机制没有改变。改变的是，代理的目的是评估的一部分，也是事后记录所证明的一部分。”无论你的AI应用进程处于哪个阶段，在数据层的强制执行都能让你更快而非更慢地推进。这些控制本来就在数据库里。不同之处在于，代理如今必须穿过它们。

这是一根数字围绳，而不是一扇锁死的门。目标不是阻止代理做有用的事，而是界定代理能走多远、能碰什么、能改什么、什么情况需要升级，以及在出错时组织如何重建事件经过。以这种方式治理的代理，具备身份、边界、监控和可审计性。企业可以更快地采纳它们，因为安全、风险和管理层信任其底层的运营模式。

这套方案建立在开源Postgres之上，这种开放基础使企业始终掌控数据存放位置、谁能接触、依据何种策略，而不会把治理权让渡给一个自己不拥有或无法检查的层级。对于受监管行业而言，数据主权与源端强制执行的结合并非锦上添花，而是将代理投入生产的先决条件。代理系统会越来越强大、越来越自主。这恰恰是审慎思考控制权归属的理由，而非放慢脚步的理由。在数据层实施治理的企业，可以在AI上大步前进，因为保护数据的，早已不止是一厢情愿。

EDB Postgres AI是一个开源的、企业级、主权数据与AI平台，统一了事务、分析和AI工作负载，并在数据所在之处强制执行治理。完整框架可参见EDB白皮书《Governing Agentic AI at Enterprise Speed》。作者为EDB首席技术官Max Romanenko。

items.title: Resurrected RTX 3060 12GB price jumps 45% in the two months since it was revived — 2021-era GPU now costs nearly $500 across most retailers
items.description: The RTX 3060 12GB was revived to offer consumers a budget GPU with a relatively large VRAM pool, but it has succumbed to the same fate as every other SKU like it. Launched at around $330, most variants now cost close to $500.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 10 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Nvidia ostensibly brought back the RTX 3060 12GB in late June to help gamers cope with the ongoing component crisis. Since most of the world's memory is being routed to expensive AI chips, the RTX 3060 12GB offered gamers a 12GB VRAM pool for what was supposed to be a reasonable price... if only the price remained steady. As of today, this five-year-old GPU now costs almost $500 across the world, which is just as much as the RTX 5060.MSI's Ventus 2X OC variant of the RTX 3060 12GB launched at just $300 on its online store and $340 on Newegg. It's now listed for $480 in both places. That's a 60% increase in less than two months, compared to its lowest price. Similarly, Asus' Dual V2 OC variant was released with a $330 MSRP, which quickly rose to $360 on Newegg, and the same card is now sitting at $500, constituting a 52% price hike from launch.The cheapest RTX 3060 12GB right now, the Gigabyte Windforce OC Rev 2.0 model, currently costs $460, up 35% from the $340 it arrived at in late June. The same GPU is listed for 417 GBP on Amazon UK, which converts to $566. In Europe, the cheapest variant is once again Asus' Dual V2 OC, costing 386 EUR on Amazon Germany, or roughly $450; price aggregator Geizhals says it was just 330 EUR a month ago.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: In comparison, the RTX 5060, which is two generations newer, can be easily had for around $450 from a bunch of different vendors. That GPU is not only significantly faster but also more efficient, while carrying the latest features such as DLSS multi-frame gen support. In our GPU hierarchy, the 5060 is actually just as powerful as the RTX 3070 at 1080p and 1440p, and it carries the same amount of VRAM, 8GB.That VRAM capacity is the only thing going for the 3060 12GB at this point, and even with extra memory to utilize, the GPU isn't really capable enough to deliver better performance in games. Plus, you can find better deals on the used market, or even renewed offers from big retailers, so the re-launched RTX 3060 12GB just doesn't make sense from any angle right now, despite its still-decent 1080p chops. You may like Legacy Nvidia RTX 3060 12GB returns to retail five years after original launch, priced at $339 Nvidia relaunches the RTX 3060 with 12GB of VRAM to fight the AI crisis GeForce RTX 50-series GPU prices spike as much as 39% as Blackwell price hikes hit the US The 3060 is cheaper to produce for Nvidia, thanks to its slower GDDR6 memory compared to the GDDR7 you get on the 5060. It's fabricated on the older, less in-demand 8nm node from Samsung, compared to TSMC's N5, which should also help with yield. But none of those manufacturing leniencies seem to be trickling down to the customer. Even the RTX 5050, which can be had for $300, is faster than the revived RTX 3060 12GB. items.author: Hassam Nasir
items.titleZh: Resurrected RTX 3060 12GB price jumps 45% in the two months since it was revived — 2021-era GPU now costs nearly $500 across most retailers
items.descriptionZh:
Nvidia 在六月底重新上架了 RTX 3060 12GB 显卡，本意是帮助游戏玩家应对持续已久的电子元件供应危机。由于全球大部分显存产能都被调配给价格昂贵的 AI 芯片，这款五年前的老卡凭借 12GB 显存容量，被视为一个以合理价格满足玩家需求的“救市”方案——前提是价格能保持稳定。然而事与愿违，如今这款老 GPU 的全球售价已普遍逼近 500 美元，几乎与新一代的 RTX 5060 持平。

具体来看，微星 Ventus 2X OC 版本的 RTX 3060 12GB 最初在官方商店售价 300 美元，新蛋网售价 340 美元，现在两个渠道都已涨至 480 美元，相比最低点涨幅达 60%。华硕 Dual V2 OC 版本的发布价为 330 美元，新蛋网很快涨到 360 美元，如今已标价 500 美元，涨幅高达 52%。目前最便宜的型号是技嘉 Windforce OC Rev 2.0，现价 460 美元，比六月底上市时的 340 美元上涨了 35%。在英国亚马逊，同款卡标价 417 英镑，折合约 566 美元；在欧洲，最便宜的仍是华硕 Dual V2 OC，德国亚马逊售价 386 欧元，约合 450 美元，而价格聚合网站 Geizhals 显示一个月前仅为 330 欧元。

作为对比，两代新出的 RTX 5060 目前可以轻松以 450 美元左右的价格从多家零售商处买到。这款显卡不仅性能明显更强、能效更高，还支持 DLSS 多帧生成等最新技术。根据 Tom's Hardware 的 GPU 性能层级，RTX 5060 在 1080p 和 1440p 下的性能与 RTX 3070 相当，同样配备 8GB 显存。也就是说，RTX 3060 12GB 目前唯一的优势只剩下显存容量，但即便有更多的显存可用，它的核心性能也不足以在实际游戏中带来更好的帧率表现。更何况，二手市场或大型零售商的翻新渠道都有更划算的选择，因此这款重新上架的 RTX 3060 12GB 即使 1080p 游戏表现尚可，从任何角度来看都谈不上划算。

从生产成本分析，RTX 3060 对于 Nvidia 来说更便宜：它使用的是较慢的 GDDR6 显存，而 RTX 5060 采用 GDDR7；此外，3060 基于三星较旧的 8nm 制程，相比台积电 N5 工艺，产能利用率更高、成本更低。但所有这些制造成本上的优势，似乎都没有传递给消费者。更讽刺的是，售价 300 美元的 RTX 5050，性能也比这款重获新生的 RTX 3060 12GB 更快。

history.content: Google’s AI note-taking app, Gemini Notebook, can now pull information from the books you’ve purchased. The new “Expert Intelligence” feature allows you to bring titles from Google Play Books directly into Gemini Notebook, which means you can ask questions about the material, as well as generate plans, infographics, AI podcasts, and more based on their contents.During a briefing with The Verge, Google Labs editorial director Steven Johnson showed how you can use the tool to generate a recipe book using the information in Michael Pollan’s Food Rules. In another example, Gemini Notebook applied the knowledge from Kim Scott’s management-focused Radical Candor to answer a question about handling a difficult conversation with an employee. You’ll also be able to view the full text of the book directly in Notebook.To start, more than 100,000 books from publishers like Penguin Random House, Johns Hopkins University Press, Macmillan Publishers, O’Reilly Media, and others will support Expert Intelligence. Google also worked with 15 authors, including Pollan, Scott, Steven Pinker, and Jennifer Wallace, to create “Featured Notebooks” that each author customizes with additional source material, intro letters, and more. Titles that support the feature will have “Gemini Notebook” listed under the “Tools” badge in Google Play Books.“I’m really interested in the idea of building a collection of people whose work you really value, and kind of creating your own dream team of advisors that are just available to you wherever you go,” Johnson says.Additionally, Google built protections into Gemini Notebook to prevent other users from accessing material from books they haven’t purchased. If you share a Notebook that includes a purchased book, a user who doesn’t own the title will see it listed as a source, but they won’t be able to view the full text or information related to it. Clicking the source will direct users to Google Play Books, where they can purchase it.RelatedGemini gets notebooks to help you organize projectsGoogle is renaming NotebookLM to Gemini Notebook“We want to be able to create a space where users can bring whatever knowledge, whatever expertise they think is going to be most relevant and do it in a way that creates new revenue possibilities for authors and publishers as well,” Johnson says.Google will eventually bring this feature to AI Mode in Search and the Gemini app, both of which can already pull information from Gemini Notebook. The company also has plans to expand Expert Intelligence to support scholarly articles, magazine articles, and newspapers, according to Johnson.
history.author: Emma Roth
history.titleZh: 谷歌的人工智能笔记应用现在允许你与书籍互动
history.descriptionZh:
谷歌旗下AI笔记应用Gemini Notebook推出了一项名为“专家智能”（Expert Intelligence）的新功能，允许用户将已购买的Google Play Books电子书直接导入Notebook，从而基于书籍内容提问、生成计划、信息图、AI播客等。在《The Verge》的演示中，Google Labs编辑总监Steven Johnson展示了如何利用Michael Pollan《食物规则》中的信息生成食谱书，以及如何运用Kim Scott的管理学著作《极度坦诚》回答关于与员工进行艰难对话的问题。用户还能在Notebook中直接查看书籍全文。

初期将有超过10万本图书支持该功能，合作出版商包括Penguin Random House、Johns Hopkins University Press、Macmillan Publishers、O'Reilly Media等。Google还携手Pollan、Scott、Steven Pinker、Jennifer Wallace等15位作者打造了“精选笔记本”（Featured Notebooks），每位作者会补充额外资料、介绍信等内容。支持该功能的书籍会在Google Play Books的“工具”徽章下标注“Gemini Notebook”标识。

Johnson表示，他对构建一个由自己珍视的著作作者组成的“智囊团”概念很感兴趣，这相当于随时随地拥有理想的顾问团队。为保护版权，Google在Gemini Notebook中设置了防护机制：若用户分享包含已购书籍的笔记本，未购买该书的用户只能看到来源列表，无法查看全文或相关信息，点击来源会被引导至Google Play Books购买。

Johnson强调，该功能旨在让用户汇聚所需知识，同时为作者和出版商创造新的收入可能。未来，Google计划将该功能扩展至搜索中的AI模式及Gemini应用（两者已能从Gemini Notebook读取信息），并支持学术文章、杂志文章和报纸内容。

history.title: Jensen Huang says Nvidia achieved AGI, again — not that it matters
history.description:
On Nvidia's earnings call Wednesday, CEO Jensen Huang casually announced the company had "achieved AGI," one of the tech industry's ultimate goals some of its biggest players have spent years chasing. Almost immediately, Huang dismissed the coveted milestone as "senseless."   
He's right. For the supposed finish line of the AI race, there is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we'll know when we've actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary. 
Asked about OpenAI's pursuit of AGI, Huang said that when it comes to Nvidia, "for many tasks, we could say that we've already achieved AGI."  …
Read the full story at The Verge.
history.content: On Nvidia’s earnings call Wednesday, CEO Jensen Huang casually announced the company had “achieved AGI,” one of the tech industry’s ultimate goals some of its biggest players have spent years chasing. Almost immediately, Huang dismissed the coveted milestone as “senseless.”He’s right. For the supposed finish line of the AI race, there is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we’ll know when we’ve actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary.Asked about OpenAI’s pursuit of AGI, Huang said that when it comes to Nvidia, “for many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.” He did not provide a precise definition or benchmark, but added, “I think of all of those milestones and all those, you know, they’re kind of senseless at this point.” He also pointed to AI moving beyond responding to simple prompts to autonomous agents capable of learning new skills and improving themselves “recursively.” What really matters, Huang said, is that AI is “doing productive and useful work” and “generating profitable tokens,” with more compute producing more tokens — and, inevitably, more profit. “This is the exact phase where we’re at. Which is the reason why everybody’s leaning in.”“… for many tasks, we could say that we’ve already achieved AGI.”This isn’t the first time Huang has said we’ve reached AGI. In March, during an appearance on the Lex Fridman podcast, he plainly stated, “I think we’ve achieved AGI.” Huang didn’t say exactly what he meant by AGI. Fridman proposed his own oddly specific definition: an AI system that’s able to “essentially do your job,” as in start, grow, and run a successful tech company worth more than $1 billion. Walking back his earlier claims, Huang said that “the odds of 100,000 of those agents building Nvidia is zero percent.”RelatedNvidia is about to be a hundred-billion-dollar-a-quarter companyNvidia CEO Jensen Huang says ‘I think we’ve achieved AGI’AI companies are sick of their favorite buzzword — so they’re inventing new onesOver the years, other tech leaders have capitalized on the term’s fuzziness and produced a veritable grab bag of definitions and benchmarks, all orbiting the same nebulous concept: AI capable of matching or surpassing human intelligence across a broad range of domains, despite the fact that “intelligence” also doesn’t have a universally agreed-upon definition.There is no consensus on what artificial general intelligence means, let alone how we’ll know when we’ve actually got there, which makes achieving it equally arbitrary. The definition of AGI according to OpenAI – a company founded with the explicit goal of building it – leaves a lot of room for interpretation. In its charter, OpenAI defines AGI as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” Altman himself has acknowledged that this is hardly a measurable standard, admitting last year that AGI is “not a super useful term.” Complicating matters is OpenAI’s different, financially-driven definition of AGI it worked out with Microsoft — reportedly systems that can generate at least $100 billion in profits. In a recent Time story, chief research officer Mark Chen estimated OpenAI is “80% of the way” to AGI, while Altman said that by the end of the year the company would have something he would call AGI.The fact that both AGI and its threshold remain undefined is no secret: tech leaders say so themselves, even as they make predictions predicated on it. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called AGI “imprecise,” even a “marketing term,” preferring instead to talk about “powerful AI.” Others have similarly reached for their own terms to describe broadly similar ideas. In theory, there are supposed to be distinctions between them, but in practice they all bleed together. Meta talks about “personal superintelligence,” Microsoft “humanist superintelligence,” and Amazon “useful general intelligence.” Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis has taken to talking about how we’ve arrived at the “foothills of the singularity.” And OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, who reportedly led employees in chants of “feel the AGI,” now runs a company called Safe Superintelligence.New terminology hasn’t made the meaning more tangible.New terminology hasn’t made the meaning more tangible. So long as AGI remains poorly defined and carelessly used, the whole thing is senseless. Well, unless you want a handy tool for hyping up progress. So expect the industry — Huang included — to keep the AGI talk coming. Maybe an AGI will eventually show up and tell us what AGI actually means.
history.author: Robert Hart
history.titleZh: Jensen Huang says Nvidia achieved AGI, again — not that it matters
history.descriptionZh:
英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋在周三的财报电话会议上语出惊人，宣布公司“已经实现了AGI（通用人工智能）”——这一科技行业顶级玩家们追逐多年的终极目标。然而话音刚落，他又随即否定了这一里程碑的意义，称其“毫无意义”。他的判断是对的：对于这场AI竞赛的所谓终点线，业界从未就通用人工智能的含义达成共识，更不用说如何判断我们是否真正抵达了终点，这使得“实现AGI”本身就变得同样武断。

当被问及OpenAI对AGI的追求时，黄仁勋表示，就英伟达而言，“对于许多任务，我们可以说已经实现了AGI。”他没有给出精确的定义或基准，但补充道：“我认为所有这些里程碑，你知道，在这一点上都有点毫无意义。”他还指出，AI正从响应简单提示词，演进到能够自主学习新技能并“递归式”自我改进的自主智能体。黄仁勋强调，真正重要的是AI正在“做有生产力和有用的工作”并“生成能盈利的token”，更多的算力产生更多的token——不可避免地带来更多利润。“这正是我们目前所处的阶段，也是所有人都在全力投入的原因。”

这并非黄仁勋首次宣称我们已达到AGI。今年3月，他在Lex Fridman播客节目中曾直言“我认为我们已实现了AGI”，但并未明确其含义。当时Fridman提出了一个异常具体的定义：一个能够“完成你的工作”的AI系统，即创办、发展并运营一家市值超过10亿美元的成功科技公司。黄仁勋随后收回了此前的说法，表示“10万个这样的智能体打造出英伟达的概率是零”。

多年来，其他科技领袖也充分利用了AGI这一术语的模糊性，产出了五花八门的定义和基准，但都围绕着同一个模糊概念：在广泛领域中能够匹配或超越人类智能的AI——尽管“智能”本身也没有一个被普遍接受的定义。OpenAI创立时的明确目标是构建AGI，其章程将AGI定义为“在大多数具有经济价值的工作中表现优于人类的高度自主系统”。但联合创始人兼CEO奥特曼自己也承认，这很难算是一个可衡量的标准，去年他甚至表示AGI“不是一个非常有用的术语”。更复杂的是，OpenAI与微软之间达成了一套以财务为导向的AGI定义——据报道是指能够创造至少1000亿美元利润的系统。在最近《时代》杂志的报道中，OpenAI首席研究官马克·陈估计公司已“完成了通向AGI的80%”，而奥特曼则表示到年底公司会拥有他称之为AGI的东西。

AGI及其门槛都未被定义这一事实并非秘密：科技领袖们自己就承认了这一点，即便他们仍基于此做出预测。Anthropic CEO达里奥·阿莫德伊称AGI“不精确”，甚至是“营销术语”，他更倾向于谈论“强大AI”。其他公司也各自创造了术语来描述大致相似的概念——理论上它们应有区别，但实际上已混为一谈：Meta谈论“个人超级智能”，微软谈“人本超级智能”，亚马逊谈“实用通用智能”。谷歌DeepMind的戴密斯·哈萨比斯则常谈论我们已抵达“奇点的山麓”。OpenAI联合创始人伊利亚·苏茨克维——据报道曾带领员工高呼“感受AGI”——如今经营着一家名为“安全超级智能”的公司。

但新的术语并未让含义变得更加具体。只要AGI仍然定义不清、使用随意，整件事就毫无意义——除非你想要一个方便的工具来炒作进展。因此可以预见，包括黄仁勋在内的整个行业会继续大谈AGI。也许有一天，一个真正的AGI会出现，并告诉我们AGI到底意味着什么。

history.title: Trump administration weighs expanding chip tariffs to laptops, consoles, and servers, report claims — January's data center exemptions may be scrapped
history.description: The Trump administration is weighing a second round of semiconductor tariffs that would extend duties beyond chips to products built with them.
history.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 14 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The Trump administration is weighing a second round of semiconductor tariffs that would extend duties beyond chips to products built with them, including laptops, gaming consoles, and data center servers, eight unnamed sources familiar with the talks told POLITICO in a report published today. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick favors a structure that would cap duty-free chip imports at a volume pegged to each company's committed U.S. production, four of the sources said, and Commerce officials have indicated in private talks that the exemptions attached to January's 25% tariff, which cover data centers, R&D, startups, and consumer devices, may not carry over. A phase-in period is under discussion, and the framework could still change substantially in the coming weeks.Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs (Image credit: tsmc)While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply marketThe state of China's decade-long semiconductor pushHuawei Ascend NPU roadmap examined China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fabChina's latest round of rare-earth export controls explainedProclamation 11002, signed on January 14, imposed a 25% duty on a narrow set of advanced accelerators, with Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X named in the accompanying White House fact sheet, and explicitly labeled the action Phase 1.The same document directed Commerce to report to the president by July 1 on the market for semiconductors used in U.S. data centers, and a separate April 14 report from the USTR and Commerce covered tariff negotiations with Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan. The exemption categories now in question match those written into the January action and include U.S. data centers, research and development, startups, repairs, non-data-center consumer and industrial applications, and public sector uses.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Taiwan's January trade agreement applies zero tariffs on Taiwanese chips within 2.5 times a company's current U.S. manufacturing capacity while new plants are under construction, tightening to 1.5 times once they're built. TSMC has committed $265 billion to its Arizona site, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history, yet projects only around 30% of its most advanced capacity there at full build-out, according to POLITICO. Taiwan produces more than 90% of the world's leading-edge chips, and industry representatives argued in the talks that a quota keyed to current domestic capacity can't cover the volumes hyperscalers are buying during a record AI spending run.Jonathan McHale, digital policy chief at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, whose members include Amazon, Google, and Meta, compared the data center buildout to "building the transcontinental railroad" and said added cost and unpredictability put that investment at risk. You may like Taiwan weighs criminal ban on AI chip exports to all of China While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market Industry coalition urges Trump administration to take urgent action as AI data centers' extreme memory consumption threatens other industries Tech lobbyists have met with Lutnick and Bureau of Industry and Security undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler with growing frequency since the start of summer, per the report, but three of the sources said recent talks moved against the industry. One person involved put the domestic manufacturing build-out at more than five years, longer than any phase-in the administration has allowed on previous tariff rounds.White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the approach, saying reshoring chip manufacturing is a top priority for the president; the Commerce Department didn't respond to POLITICO's requests for comment.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.

history.titleZh: 报道称特朗普政府考虑将芯片关税扩大至笔记本电脑、游戏机和服务器——1月的数据中心豁免或被取消
history.descriptionZh:
特朗普政府正酝酿第二轮半导体关税，其范围将从芯片本身扩展至使用芯片的终端产品，包括笔记本电脑、游戏主机和数据中心服务器。据POLITICO今日报道，八位匿名知情人士透露了相关讨论细节。商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克倾向于一种配额机制：以各企业承诺的美国本土产量为基准，设定一个免税芯片进口上限，超过部分需缴纳关税。商务部官员在私下会谈中还暗示，今年1月25%关税中附带的多项豁免——涵盖数据中心、研发、初创企业及消费设备——可能不会延续。目前正在讨论分阶段实施的时间表，但整个框架在未来数周内仍可能发生重大变化。

这场关税风波源于1月14日签署的第11002号公告，该公告对一小部分先进加速器征收25%关税，英伟达H200和AMD MI325X被明确点名，白宫称其为“第一阶段”行动。该公告同时要求商务部在7月1日前向总统提交关于美国数据中心所用半导体市场的报告，而4月14日美国贸易代表办公室和商务部联合发布的报告则涉及与台湾、韩国和日本的关税谈判。如今受到质疑的豁免类别，正是1月行动中写入的那些，包括美国数据中心、研发、初创企业、维修、非数据中心消费与工业应用以及公共部门用途。

台湾方面，1月签署的贸易协议规定，在新建工厂建设期间，台湾芯片可享受相当于企业当前美国产能2.5倍进口量的零关税待遇，工厂建成后这一倍数将收紧至1.5倍。台积电已承诺向亚利桑那州投资2650亿美元，这是美国历史上最大规模的外国直接投资，但据POLITICO报道，其最先进产能全面投产后，在美占比也仅约30%。台湾生产了全球超过90%的先进制程芯片。行业代表在谈判中指出，在AI支出创纪录的当下，以现有国内产能为基准的配额，根本无法覆盖超大规模云服务商的采购量。

计算机与通信行业协会（CCIA）数字政策主管乔纳森·麦克海尔将数据中心建设比作“建造横贯大陆的铁路”，并表示额外成本和不可预测性正使这项投资面临风险。该协会成员包括亚马逊、谷歌和Meta。自入夏以来，科技游说团体与卢特尼克及工业与安全局副局长杰弗里·凯斯勒的会面频率不断上升，但三位知情人士称，最近的会谈风向对行业不利。一位参与者指出，美国本土制造能力的全面构建需要五年以上，这远超此前各轮关税中政府允许的任何分阶段过渡期。

白宫发言人库什·德赛为这一做法辩护，称将芯片制造回流是美国总统的首要任务；商务部则未回应POLITICO的置评请求。这场围绕关税结构、豁免范围和实施节奏的博弈，不仅将决定芯片进口成本，更可能重塑全球半导体供应链格局——尤其是对高度依赖台湾先进制程的英伟达、AMD等美国芯片巨头，以及大规模采购AI加速器的云计算产业。特朗普政府此番“芯片+终端”双重关税的设计，名义上旨在强制推动制造业回流，但其对AI基础设施投资、消费电子价格乃至全球科技产业链的连锁影响，仍有待观察。

history.title: Hot Chips 2026: Cerebras lays out the future of wafer-scale AI — Nexus system architecture triples rack-scale performance, CS-6 wafer to incorporate stacked DRAM
history.description: At Hot Chips 2026, Cerebras revealed the next two generations of its wafer-scale accelerator roadmap. It also discussed the benefits of its new Nexus rack design for the CS-4 rack-scale accelerator and the performance of the three WS-3T wafer-scale engines contained within.
history.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Cerebras' SRAM-packed wafer-scale engines (WSEs) have carved out a niche in the AI model serving space for extremely low-latency, high-throughput inference, enabling services like OpenAI's ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast tier. At Hot Chips 2026, the company revealed the next two generations of its wafer-scale accelerator roadmap. It also discussed the benefits of its new Nexus rack design for the CS-4 rack-scale accelerator and the performance of the three WS-3T wafer-scale engines contained within.The integration of a huge coherent processor on a single massive slice of silicon is a unique feat in the industry. But that approach also comes with limitations. AI demands for memory are only increasing due to growing model sizes (the memory occupancy of which can be amortized across multiple inference sessions) and ever-lengthening contexts stored in large KV caches (which are also unique to each inference session).Traditional GPU makers have addressed those pressures, in part by working with memory makers to stack HBM higher and by using more of it per accelerator to expand that precious resource in proximity to the processor. But on a wafer-scale design whose area is already 100% utilized by logic and memory, adding more of a particular resource requires giving up area that might have been used for some other purpose. Since silicon production will continue to take place on 300mm wafers for the foreseeable future, Cerebras must look in other directions to scale up the on-chip resources available to its processors.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: (Image credit: Cerebras)Cerebras revealed that it will start expanding its wafer-scale engines into stacked designs with its CS-6 system’s WSE, currently two generations out on its roadmap. For the first time, Cerebras will attempt 3D stacking of DRAM on top of its logic and SRAM wafer, a move it claims will maintain the company's performance lead for inference while reducing the area required for the overall chip.The goal of stacking wafer-scale logic and memory chips on top of one another is certainly ambitious, but it’s only one potentially important change in the CS-6 system. The concurrent reduction in area Cerebras foresees suggests the company might be able to increase the overall number of WSEs it produces, which could relax a crucial constraint as the company seeks to scale its business amid a world of ever-increasing wafer demand. You may like AMD and Cerebras partner on low-latency, high-throughput AI inference Hot Chips 2026: d-Matrix stacks AI accelerator directly on custom DRAM for 100 TB/s per card Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia presents Groq 3 LPX architecture and unveils its first third-party inference benchmark (Image credit: Cerebras)In the present, Cerebras is boosting the performance of its existing wafer-scale platform with its new CS-4 rack-scale system and its Nexus rack design. CS-4 incorporates three of the company's refreshed WS-3T wafers into self-contained "backpacks" that incorporate power delivery, scale-up networking, and liquid cooling infrastructure into a single pluggable module. (Image credit: Cerebras)Cerebras notes that because these modules are self-contained, future wafer-scale engines built with this architecture can be swapped in without exchanging the entire rack in the process.Cerebras chief system architect JP Fricker had choice words when describing the 5,000 cables that are used to connect the Rubin NVL72 NVLink scale-up domain within each of those racks, calling it "a mess" and contrasting it with the cleaner and less failure-prone design provided by the on-die interconnects and self-contained compute module design of the Nexus system. (Image credit: Cerebras)The Nexus backpack design also disaggregates the I/O interfaces of the WSE from the rest of the backpack's components. Two I/O modules now connect to the edges of the wafer, providing RoCE v2 RDMA connections for interoperability with other systems, alongside a direct connection to other wafers in the rack. Because these modules are also interchangeable, they provide another potential route for future upgrades, independent of the core compute wafer. (Image credit: Cerebras)The Nexus design situates up to 10 rack power delivery units for each backpack at the front side of the rack, each group of which can be configured for varying levels of redundancy in accordance with an operator’s needs. The rack also provides air cooling for the backpack components that need it. What to read next Hot Chips 2026: Intel dives deep on Crescent Island AI accelerator TSMC says panel packaging won't replace CoWoS anytime soon for the largest future AI processors Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia breaks down 88-core Vera CPU (Image credit: Cerebras)Mounting the wafer-scale engines vertically in the backpack modules lets Cerebras do away with a PCB or substrate for the wafer to handle all its supporting infrastructure. Instead, the backpack connects the large copper busbar that delivers juice to the chip directly to its back side. This close contact is important, as it minimizes power losses that occur on the way to the chip, as happens with a BGA GPU chip mounted on a PCB module with all of its power delivery circuitry located around the die.Cerebras translates the power saved this way directly into performance in the WS-3T. The company says the losses avoided by the Nexus backpack design allow it to deliver twice as much power to the wafer-scale engine as in past designs, which leads directly to increased clock speeds and up to twice the performance of the WS-3. (Image credit: Cerebras)Using the same base silicon as the WS-3, each WS-3T delivers twice as many sparse FP16 petaFLOPS and twice as much memory bandwidth from its SRAM. But the WS3-T is still limited to 44GB of memory across the entire wafer, and three such wafers in a CS-4 rack only scale up to 132 GB, far less than the 20.7 TB of HBM in the Vera Rubin NVL72 system and the 31 TB of AMD’s Helios.The company doesn’t publish dense PFLOPS figures for these engines, possibly because the dataflow architectural design of the chips is specifically built to derive advantage from sparsity in a way a traditional GPU usually isn’t. (Image credit: Cerebras)In any event, to accommodate the larger models of today and tomorrow, Cerebras will need to scale up and out. But unlike other rack-scale systems that rely on Ethernet for scale-out, Cerebras can simply connect CS-4 systems together using the same wafer-to-wafer interconnect that connects wafer-scale engines together in the Nexus rack. The company claims 2.4 Tb/s of direct scale-up bandwidth per wafer within the rack for a total of 7.2 Tb/s of inter-chip bandwidth at 2 μs latencies.Cerebras notes that with its architecture, only the model activations need to pass between wafer-scale engines, so the relatively low bandwidth of the direct wafer connection isn't the obstacle to scaling out the system that it might seem when evaluated against the hundreds of terabytes per second of scale-up bandwidth of a system like Vera Rubin NVL72 or AMD's Helios. (The on-die fabric of the WSE-3T boasts 53.4 PB/s of bandwidth, regardless.) (Image credit: Cerebras)The CS-4 system architecture lays the groundwork for the next-generation CS-5 accelerator, which will use new WSE silicon in 2027. For smaller models, the company says the next-generation WSE will deliver up to 10,000 tokens per second per user, while larger frontier models from labs like DeepSeek or OpenAI could run at 5,000 tokens per second per user.As Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said, AI agents are impatient, and the ability to provide such vast numbers of tokens per second using specialized accelerators like the CS-4 will likely continue to be an important niche for Cerebras to exploit alongside its partners at OpenAI and AMD going forward.
